purpose: Clean transcriptions of Marrow ED8 source-detail paragraphs whose scanned OCR carried figure-label debris, page markers, broken words and solutions belonging to the next question. The reviewed takeaway paragraph, emphasis and rationales are unchanged; only the source-detail text after the takeaway is replaced. Figure-only labels are dropped, tables printed in the source are rebuilt as structured tables, and checked against the page images where the scan was unreadable.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q009.displayText:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a medial lemniscus tract lesion following a high-voltage electrical injury. The medial lemniscus is formed by the internal arcuate fibres. It is also called Reil's ribbon.

The internal arcuate fibres are axons of the second-order neurons from the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus. In the upper medulla, they decussate and form the medial lemniscus, which synapses in the thalamus.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q010.displayText:
The marked structure is the olive. The olive is seen in the medulla. The external features of the medulla oblongata are:

Anteriorly, the anterior median fissure is continuous with the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord. On either side of the fissure are pyramids containing the corticospinal tracts. Posterolateral to the pyramids are the olives. Olives are elevations produced by the underlying inferior olivary nuclei. Posterior to the olives, the inferior cerebellar peduncles connect the medulla with the cerebellum.

Posteriorly, the superior half forms the floor of the fourth ventricle. Inferiorly, there is a posterior median sulcus. On either side of this sulcus, the nucleus gracilis is situated. The nucleus cuneatus lies lateral to the nucleus gracilis.

The anterolateral sulcus lies in the groove between the pyramid and the olive, and the XII cranial nerve emerges from there. The posterolateral sulcus lies in the groove between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle. The IX, X, and XI cranial nerves emerge from here.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q007.displayText: The image shows a histopathological section of the cerebellum. The cells marked with the arrow are Purkinje cells, and they inhibit deep nuclei of the cerebellum.

marrow__ANAT_CH25_Q014.displayText:
Thrombosis of the superior cerebellar artery causes a cerebellar lesion, which presents with ataxia and incoordination.

Blood supply of cerebellum:
• Superior cerebellar artery
• Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
• Anterior inferior cerebellar artery

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q001.displayText:
The renal angle lies between the lower border of the 12th rib and the lateral border of erector spinae.

The given clinical scenario and the renal angle tenderness are suggestive of acute pyelonephritis. The renal angle is formed by the lower border of the 12th rib and the lateral border of the erector spinae.

The lower pole of the kidney occupies this angle. Tenderness in this angle is usually suggestive of infection in and around the kidney, or of renal stones.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q002.displayText:
The costovertebral angle is formed by the 12th rib and the vertebral column; tenderness there can accompany renal disease.

The angle shown in the image is the costovertebral angle, formed between the lower border of the 12th rib and the vertebral column.

Causes of pain/tenderness at the costovertebral angle include:
• Nephrolithiasis
• Pelviureteric junction obstruction
• Pyelonephritis
• Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Hantavirus

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q004.displayText:
Lateroconal fascia extends laterally from the perirenal fascia and joins the parietal peritoneum.

The lateroconal fascia attaches the perirenal fascia to the peritoneum. It extends from the lateral margin of the perirenal fascia and attaches to the parietal peritoneum.

Option A: Gerota's fascia is the perirenal fascia. The kidney and the suprarenal gland are enclosed within the anterior and posterior laminae of the perirenal fascia. The anterior lamina of the perirenal fascia blends with the connective tissue surrounding the great vessels behind the duodenum and pancreas. The posterior lamina continues as the lateroconal fascia.

Option C: Thoracolumbar fascia is a complex arrangement of multiple fascial layers in the thoracolumbar region. This fascia encloses the paraspinal muscles, the quadratus lumborum muscle and the latissimus dorsi muscle.

Option D: Treitz's fascia has been used to refer to the fusion fascia behind the head of the pancreas.

Coverings around the kidney, from inside out: perinephric fat, perirenal fascia, and paranephric fat.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q007.displayText:
The marked area on the left kidney faces the stomach, an anterior relation of the left kidney.

The marked area in the image of the left kidney is related to the stomach.

Anterior relations of the kidneys:

The posterior relations of the kidneys:
• One vessel: subcostal vessels
• Two ligaments: medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
• Three nerves: subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves
• Four muscles: diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis
• The right kidney is related to the 12th rib, and the left kidney is related to the 11th and 12th ribs.

displayTables.title: Anterior relations of the kidneys
rows: Right suprarenal gland; 2nd part of duodenum; hepatic flexure of colon
Left suprarenal gland; pancreas; splenic vessels; splenic flexure and beginning of descending colon

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q008.displayText:
The liver-facing area (label 1) on the right kidney is separated from the liver by peritoneum because the kidney is retroperitoneal.

The anterior surface of the right kidney related to the right lobe of the liver (marked as 1) is separated from it by a layer of peritoneum. As the kidneys are retroperitoneal, their intraperitoneal anterior relations are separated from them by a peritoneal layer.

displayTables.title: Anterior relations of the right kidney
rows: Right suprarenal gland; 2nd part of duodenum; hepatic flexure of colon

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q009.displayText:
The sympathetic chain is not a direct posterior relation of the kidney; posterior relations include psoas, quadratus lumborum, diaphragm and nerves.

The marked structure in the given image is the left kidney. The sympathetic chain is not a posterior relation of the left kidney.

The posterior relations of the kidneys are as follows:
• One vessel: subcostal vessels
• Two ligaments: medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
• Three nerves: subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves
• Four muscles: diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis
• The right kidney is related to the 12th rib, and the left kidney is related to the 11th and 12th ribs.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q010.displayText:
At the renal hilum, structures from anterior to posterior are renal vein → renal artery → renal pelvis.

The marked area is the hilum of the kidney. It transmits the following structures, from anterior to posterior:
• Renal vein
• Renal artery
• Renal pelvis

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q011.displayText:
Renal papillae project into minor calyces, which join to form major calyces and then the renal pelvis.

The renal papillae open into the minor calyces. The papilla is the conical apex of a renal pyramid, where the urine from the collecting ducts enters the minor calyces. The minor calyces unite to form the major calyces, which further unite to form the renal pelvis.

The kidney is divided into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The renal medulla contains many striated, conical pyramids. The base of each pyramid is peripherally located, whereas the apex is directed towards the renal sinus (hilum). The renal cortex is subcapsular and arches over the bases of the pyramids. It extends between the pyramids towards the renal sinus as the renal columns.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q012.displayText:
Renal autonomic fibers reach the kidney through the renal plexus, with contributions from the celiac plexus and aorticorenal ganglion.

The coeliac plexus contributes to the nerve supply of the kidneys.

Nerve supply of the kidney:
• Coeliac ganglion and plexus
• Aorticorenal ganglion
• Lowest thoracic splanchnic nerve
• First lumbar splanchnic nerve
• Aortic plexus

The rami from these structures form a dense autonomic network around the renal artery, called the renal plexus. They control the blood flow between the cortex and the medulla.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q013.displayText:
Nutcracker syndrome results from compression of the left renal vein between the abdominal aorta and superior mesenteric artery.

The most likely cause is compression of the left renal vein between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. This manifests as nutcracker syndrome.

Nutcracker syndrome is characterized by left renal venous hypertension, which occurs due to compression of the left renal vein between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. This is because the left renal vein lies posterior and inferior to the superior mesenteric artery.

The left renal vein is longer than the right renal vein. It runs anterior to the aorta just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery and drains into the inferior vena cava after crossing the midline.

Note: The left kidney is preferred over the right in donor nephrectomy because of the long course of the left renal vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q014.displayText:
The left subcostal vein drains toward the hemiazygos system rather than the left renal vein, so renal-vein occlusion does not obstruct it.

The left subcostal vein does not drain into the left renal vein. It drains into the hemiazygos vein. So the occlusion of the left renal vein does not impede the blood flow in the left subcostal vein.

Veins that commonly drain into the left renal vein (which in turn drains into the IVC) are:
• Left inferior phrenic (diaphragmatic) vein
• Left suprarenal (adrenal) vein
• Left gonadal vein

On the right side, all the above veins drain into the inferior vena cava directly.

Apart from the veins described above, the first and second left lumbar veins and the hemiazygos vein may drain into the left renal vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q015.displayText:
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein without crossing the midline; the left renal vein and mesenteric root do cross it.

The left gonadal vein does not cross the midline. It is formed from the pampiniform plexus of veins and drains into the left renal vein.

The left renal vein is longer than the right renal vein, and it crosses the midline anterior to the aorta. It drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The right renal vein does not cross the midline.

The accessory hemiazygos vein crosses the midline to drain into the azygos vein.

The root of the mesentery extends along a line from the duodenojejunal flexure on the left side to the sacroiliac joint on the right side. It spans a length of 15 cm and crosses the midline in its course.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q016.displayText:
A small ureteric calculus commonly lodges at the vesicoureteric junction, a narrow anatomical constriction.

The vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest part of the ureter. This is why stones as small as 2 to 3 mm get arrested at the vesicoureteric junction.

The ureter is constricted at 5 places:
1. Pelviureteric junction
2. Brim of the lesser pelvis (where it crosses the common iliac artery)
3. Point where the ureter is crossed by the ductus deferens or the broad ligament of the uterus
4. Vesicoureteric junction
5. Opening in the lateral angle of the trigone

These are regarded as the surgical constrictions of the ureter. However, only 1, 2, and 4 are the anatomical constrictions of the ureter.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q017.displayText:
The ureter lies anterior to psoas major and the genitofemoral nerve, with the common iliac bifurcation at the pelvic brim; quadratus lumborum is not a direct posterior relation.

The structure marked in the image is the ureter. Quadratus lumborum is not a posterior relation of the ureter.

Posterior relations of the ureter in the abdominal cavity are:
• Psoas major
• Genitofemoral nerve
• End of the common iliac artery or beginning of the external iliac artery

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q018.displayText:
The superior mesenteric artery does not supply the ureter; ureteric branches arise from renal, gonadal, aortic, iliac and pelvic vessels.

The superior mesenteric artery does not supply the ureters.

The ureter receives its blood supply from the following arteries:
• Renal artery
• Gonadal artery
• Common iliac artery
• Internal iliac artery
• Vesical artery
• Uterine artery
• Abdominal aorta

Among these, the branches from the renal artery and the inferior vesical artery are always constant.

Clinical note: The branch of the renal artery that supplies the ureter must be carefully preserved in renal transplantation to maintain good vascularity of the ureter.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q020.displayText:
The right suprarenal vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava; the left usually drains into the left renal vein.

The right main adrenal vein usually drains into the inferior vena cava.

The left main adrenal vein usually drains into the left renal vein. Variations are common on the right side, where the right adrenal vein may drain into the right inferior phrenic vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q021.displayText:
Mercier's bar is the interureteric mucosal fold between the two ureteric orifices at the base of the bladder trigone.

Mercier's bar (interureteric bar or interureteric ridge) is a curved fold of mucous membrane between the two ureteric orifices at the base of the bladder trigone. This fold is formed by thickening of the superior border of the trigone muscle. In cystoscopy, the interureteric ridge appears as a pale band and acts as a guide to the ureteric orifices.

The mucosal fold running from the uvula vesicae to the ureteric orifice is called Bell's bar. This fold forms the lateral border of the trigone. It contains a band of muscle fibres called Bell's muscle.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q022.displayText:
The median prostatic lobe can project at the bladder neck as the uvula vesicae, especially when enlarged.

The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae.

The uvula vesicae is an elevation in the mucous membrane of the urinary bladder, behind the internal urethral orifice. It is often enlarged in benign prostatic hypertrophy.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q023.displayText:
At birth the bladder is relatively abdominal, placing the internal urethral orifice near the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

The internal urethral orifice lies at the level of the upper border of the pubic symphysis at birth.

At birth, the bladder is an abdominal organ. As the child grows, the bladder descends, and near puberty it becomes a pelvic organ.

In an adult, the internal urethral orifice lies 3-4 cm behind the lower part of the pubic symphysis. It corresponds to the bladder neck.

Clinical note: As the bladder lies above the symphysis pubis in children, suprapubic needle puncture can safely be performed to obtain urine samples. In adults, this can only be done if the bladder is fully distended.

marrow__ANAT_CH51_Q025.displayText:
The renal artery divides into five segmental end arteries: four anterior segments and one posterior segment.

There are five arterial segments in the kidney:
• Apical
• Superior
• Middle
• Inferior
• Posterior

Blood supply of the kidney: the renal artery is a direct lateral branch of the abdominal aorta. Near the hilum of the kidney, the renal artery is divided into anterior and posterior divisions. These divisions are further divided into five segmental arteries (four anterior and one posterior). The segmental arteries further branch out in a hierarchy to form different arteries. Finally, the renal vein is formed, which joins the inferior vena cava.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q002.displayText:
The ilioinguinal nerve travels in the inguinal canal but lies outside the internal spermatic fascia and is not a spermatic-cord content.

The ilioinguinal nerve lies outside the internal spermatic fascia of the spermatic cord.

The ilioinguinal nerve is not a content of the spermatic cord, but it is a content of the inguinal canal. The ilioinguinal nerve lies inferior to the cord in the inguinal canal. It provides innervation to the groin and medial aspect of the thigh, the upper part of the scrotum, and the penile root. It may be commonly injured during open hernia repair.

The spermatic cord is a structure that passes through the inguinal canal in males. The inguinal canal is a natural passageway between the muscle layers of the anterior abdominal wall in the region of the groin. It transmits the spermatic cord in males, the round ligament of the uterus in females, and the ilioinguinal nerve in both sexes.

The contents of the spermatic cord include:
• Cremaster muscle fibers
• Testicular artery and pampiniform plexus of veins
• Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
• Vas deferens
• Cremasteric vessels
• Lymphatics
• Processus vaginalis

Coverings of the spermatic cord from inside to outside are:
• Internal spermatic fascia, from the fascia transversalis
• Cremasteric fascia
• External spermatic fascia, from the external oblique aponeurosis

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q003.displayText:
The cremasteric artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery and supplies the cremaster muscle and cord coverings.

The inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery, gives rise to the cremasteric artery. The cremasteric artery travels along with the spermatic cord to supply the cremaster muscle and the other coverings of the cord.

When the testicular artery is interrupted, collaterals form from the cremasteric and deferential arteries. This prevents ischemia of the testis.

Note: The Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy done for an undescended abdominal testis is based on this collateral formation. In the first stage, the testicular vessels are clipped laparoscopically to promote collateral formation along the vas deferens. In the second stage, the testis, along with the collaterals and the vas deferens, is mobilized to the scrotum.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q007.displayText:
Left testicular venous outflow enters the left renal vein; its obstruction can produce left varicocele and flank symptoms.

The left renal vein is likely to be occluded in this case. The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein. Occlusion of the left renal vein obstructs the outflow in the left testicular vein. As a result, the veins become swollen and cause pain on the affected side.

Venous drainage of the testis: the pampiniform plexus of veins arising from the testis ascends through the inguinal canal into the abdomen, coalescing to form the testicular vein during its course.
• The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle.
• The right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle.

Clinical note: Varicose dilatation of the veins draining the testis is called varicocele. 90% of varicoceles occur on the left side, mostly due to absence or incompetence of the valves in the testicular vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q013.displayText:
Littre glands are mucous glands embedded along the male penile urethra; Cowper glands are separate bulbourethral glands.

Littre glands are the urethral glands in males. These glands are numerous in the penile urethra. They secrete mucus prior to ejaculation, which helps in lubrication.

Option A: Cowper's glands are the bulbourethral glands found in males. They are located lateral to the membranous urethra, and each opens via a duct into the bulbar urethra by piercing the perineal membrane. Their function is to secrete mucin during sexual arousal.

Option C: Skene's glands are the paraurethral glands found in females. These open on either side of the urethra. They are considered homologous to the male prostate.

Option B: Bartholin's glands are known as the greater vestibular glands in females. These glands are located in the posterior part of the vestibule and open through a duct into the vaginal orifice. They secrete mucus during sexual arousal for lubrication.

Clinical note: Since all these glands open via a duct into the orifices, any obstruction in the duct can result in cyst formation. They can get infected and necessitate removal.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q014.displayText:
Anal carcinoma distal to the dentate line can spread to superficial inguinal nodes; testis, sigmoid colon and prostate usually drain elsewhere.

The most likely primary cause of an enlarged inguinal lymph node is anal cancer. Lymphatics from the anal canal distal to the dentate line (anal margin) drain into the inguinal lymph nodes. Hence, anal cancer arising distal to the dentate line can cause enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. Lymphatics proximal to the dentate line drain into the internal iliac lymph nodes through the superior rectal lymphatics.

Option A: In testicular cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the para-aortic lymph nodes.

Option C: In sigmoid colon cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the regional lymph nodes and then to the central lymph nodes.

Option D: In prostate cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to:
• Lymph nodes beside the internal iliac vein and in the hollow of the sacrum
• External iliac lymph nodes

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q015.displayText:
Anteversion is the angle between the cervix and vagina; anteflexion is the angle between the uterine body and cervix.

The angle of anteversion is formed between the long axis of the cervix and the long axis of the vagina.

The angle of anteflexion is formed by the body of the uterus and the long axis of the cervix.

When the whole of the uterus leans backwards at an angle to the vagina, it is called retroversion.

If the uterus angles backwards in relation to the cervix, it is called retroflexion.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q017.displayText:
The proper ovarian ligament connects the inferomedial ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus.

The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) attaches the inferomedial extremity of the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus.

Other ligamentous supports of the ovaries:
• Infundibulopelvic ligament (suspensory ligament): attaches the lateral surface of the ovary to the peritoneum lining the lateral pelvic wall. It contains the ovarian vessels and nerves.
• Mesovarium: a short peritoneal fold that attaches the ovary to the back of the broad ligament. It carries blood vessels and nerves to the hilum of the ovary.

marrow__ANAT_CH52_Q020.displayText:
The cardinal (transverse cervical/Mackenrodt) ligament extends from cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the pelvic wall.

The cardinal ligament (transverse cervical ligament or ligament of Mackenrodt) extends from the side of the cervix and the lateral fornix of the vagina to the pelvic wall.

Other ligaments of the uterus:
• Broad ligament: peritoneal fold covering the ovaries and fallopian tubes. It has three parts named after the structures it covers, i.e. mesosalpinx, mesovarium, and mesometrium (largest part).
• Pubocervical ligament: attaches the anterior aspect of the cervix and upper vagina to the posterior aspect of the pubic bones.
• Round ligaments: arise from the lateral cornua of the uterus, pass through the inguinal canal, and attach to the labia majora.
• Uterosacral ligaments: pass from the back of the uterus and cervix to the anterior surface of the sacrum.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q001.displayText:
Enzymes are generally heat-labile proteins; heating disrupts the structure needed for catalysis.

Enzymes are not heat-stable.

Most enzymes are proteins and are thus susceptible to heat. Many enzymes also have temperature ranges at which they are most active, and they get deactivated at temperatures higher than the aforementioned range.

Coenzymes are heat-stable. Enzymes are stereospecific catalysts. They are neither consumed nor permanently altered in a reaction. Most of them are proteins except ribozymes. A ribozyme is RNA with catalytic activity. Some examples of ribozymes are:
• snRNA in the spliceosome
• Ribonuclease P (RNase P)
• Peptidyl transferase

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q003.displayText:
The nitrogenase MoFe protein contains a molybdenum-bearing FeMo cofactor required for nitrogen reduction.

The prosthetic group present in dinitrogenase is molybdenum.

Prosthetic groups are the non-protein part of a holoenzyme, which are tightly and irreversibly bound to the protein part by covalent or noncovalent forces. The prosthetic group may be organic (such as a vitamin, sugar, or lipid) or inorganic (such as a metal ion). Metal ions constitute the most common type of prosthetic group.

If an enzyme uses a metal ion as a prosthetic group, it is called a metalloenzyme. Metalloenzymes have metal ions as an integral part of their structure.

Active enzyme (holoenzyme) = non-protein part + protein part (apoenzyme):
• A non-protein part that is inseparable from the protein part is a prosthetic group. An inorganic (metal) prosthetic group forms a metalloenzyme.
• A non-protein part that is separable from the protein part is called a cofactor. An organic cofactor is a coenzyme; an inorganic (metal) cofactor forms a metal-activated enzyme.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q005.displayText:
S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is a methyl donor; lipoate, ATP and vitamin K can function as coenzymes.

S-adenosyl methionine is not a coenzyme. It is a methyl group donor.

Coenzymes are cofactors in which an organic compound is present. Coenzymes transiently and reversibly bind to the enzyme to catalyze the reaction. They play an important role as a two-way shuttle.

Some coenzymes:
• Coenzyme A
• ATP/GTP
• NAD/NADP
• FAD/FMN
• Lipoic acid
• B-complex vitamins
• Vitamin C
• Vitamin K

Active enzyme (holoenzyme) = non-protein part + protein part (apoenzyme):
• A non-protein part that is inseparable from the protein part is a prosthetic group. An inorganic (metal) prosthetic group forms a metalloenzyme.
• A non-protein part that is separable from the protein part is called a cofactor. An organic cofactor is a coenzyme; an inorganic (metal) cofactor forms a metal-activated enzyme.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q006.displayText:
A metal loosely associated with an enzyme is a metal-activated cofactor; tightly bound metal characterizes a metalloenzyme.

Enzymes that use a metal ion as a cofactor are termed metal-activated enzymes (and not metalloenzymes).

Metalloenzymes have a prosthetic group in which the metal is tightly and irreversibly bound to the enzyme; the metal forms an integral part of its active structure. Metal-activated enzymes have a cofactor containing a metal (inorganic), which is loosely and reversibly bound to the enzyme. They show enhanced activity on the addition of the metal.

A cofactor is a non-protein part of a holoenzyme that can be separated from the protein part. Cofactors are mostly metal ions (inorganic). If an organic compound acts as the cofactor, it is called a coenzyme. Cofactors serve functions similar to those of prosthetic groups, but they bind in a transient, dissociable manner to enzymes, so they must be present in the medium surrounding the enzyme for catalysis to occur.

Active enzyme (holoenzyme) = protein part (apoenzyme) + non-protein part:
• Prosthetic group: inseparable from the protein part; when inorganic (metal), the enzyme is a metalloenzyme.
• Cofactor: separable from the protein part; when inorganic (metal), the enzyme is a metal-activated enzyme; when organic, the cofactor is a coenzyme.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q007.displayText:
Hydrolases cleave bonds by adding water; oxidoreductases catalyze oxidation–reduction reactions.

Hydrolases are not involved in oxidation-reduction reactions. Hydrolases are involved in the hydrolysis of the substrate using water.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q008.displayText:
Tryptophan pyrrolase (tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase) incorporates both atoms of O₂ and is a dioxygenase.

Tryptophan pyrrolase is not a mono-oxygenase. It is a di-oxygenase.

Oxygenases catalyze the incorporation of oxygen into a substrate. Oxygenases are of two types:

1. Mono-oxygenases (hydroxylases/mixed-function oxidases): incorporate one atom of oxygen into the substrate. Examples:
• Tryptophan hydroxylase
• Tyrosine hydroxylase
• Cytochrome P450
• Phenylalanine hydroxylase
• 7-alpha hydroxylase

2. Di-oxygenases: incorporate two atoms of oxygen into a substrate. Examples:
• Tryptophan pyrrolase
• Homogentisate di-oxygenase (previously known as homogentisate oxidase)

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q010.displayText:
Aldolase B is a lyase: it cleaves or forms carbon–carbon bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation.

Aldolase B is a lyase.

Lyases are enzymes that catalyze the cleavage of C-C, C-O, C-N and other covalent bonds by atom elimination, generating double bonds.

Some examples of lyases include:
• HMG-CoA lyase
• Argininosuccinate lyase
• ATP citrate lyase
• Aldolase
• Fumarase

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q013.displayText:
Isoenzymes catalyze the same reaction but differ in sequence or subunit composition, charge and electrophoretic mobility, and tissue distribution.

Isoenzymes do not have the same number of charged amino acids.

Isoenzymes are physically distinct forms of the same enzyme. They catalyze the same reaction but differ in the following:
• Amino acid sequence and the number of charged amino acids
• Subunit composition: CK-1 contains BB while CK-2 contains MB subunits
• Electrophoretic mobility: CK-1 moves faster than CK-3
• Tissue localization: CK-1 is present in the brain, CK-2 in the heart
• Substrate affinity: glucokinase has low affinity but hexokinase has high affinity

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q014.displayText:
Hemolysis releases erythrocyte LDH, particularly LDH-1 and LDH-2; the keyed isoenzyme is LDH-2.

The given scenario of a woman with fragmented RBCs and decreased RBCs is suggestive of hemolytic anemia. LDH-1 and LDH-2 isoenzymes are expressed in the RBC and are particularly raised during hemolysis.

LDH is a tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H-isoform (heart) and M-isoform (muscle).

displayTables.title: LDH isoenzymes
rows: Lungs, spleen, brain, lymphatic tissues, platelets

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q015.displayText:
After myocardial infarction, release of cardiac LDH-1 can reverse the normal serum pattern so LDH-1 exceeds LDH-2.

The given clinical scenario of sudden onset chest pain with profuse sweating and a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) with ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is suggestive of myocardial infarction. Serum LDH-1 > LDH-2 levels are seen in this condition.

Under normal conditions, LDH-2 is predominantly present in the blood and LDH-1 is predominantly present in the heart. So, normally LDH-2 > LDH-1 in blood. When cardiac tissue is damaged, LDH-1 is released into the blood, which results in a flipped lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio where LDH-1 > LDH-2.

LDH is a tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H isoform (heart) and M isoform (muscle).

displayTables.title: LDH isoenzymes
rows: Lungs, brain, lymphatic tissues, and platelets

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q016.displayText:
ALT is more liver-specific than AST in acute viral hepatocellular injury because ALT is concentrated in hepatocytes.

The enzyme most specific for his condition, acute viral hepatitis, is alanine aminotransferase (ALT).

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is predominantly found in the liver and therefore is a more specific marker for hepatocellular damage than AST.

Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) is found in various tissues. The AST/ALT ratio is very important.
• AST/ALT < 1 is seen in hepatocellular damage, as in NAFLD, toxic hepatitis and paracetamol toxicity. In cirrhosis, the ratio becomes more than 1.
• AST/ALT > 2 is suggestive, while AST/ALT > 3 is highly suggestive, of alcoholic liver disease.

Other options:

Option A: Alkaline phosphatase rise is seen in many liver diseases, but a more than fourfold rise indicates cholestasis.

Option D: GGT is used to identify occult alcohol use.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q017.displayText:
Chymotrypsinogen is the inactive zymogen precursor; activated chymotrypsin is a serine protease.

Chymotrypsinogen is a zymogen. Its active form, chymotrypsin, is a serine protease.

Serine proteases are proteolytic enzymes having serine, histidine and aspartate at the active site. The active site consists of two binding sites and a catalytic site. While serine is present in the catalytic site of serine proteases, histidine and aspartate are present on the binding sites. Serine proteases differ in substrate specificity.

Examples of serine proteases:
• Chymotrypsin
• Trypsin
• Elastase
• Thrombin
• Plasmin
• Complement proteins
• Factors X and XI
• Prostate-specific antigen

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q018.displayText:
Elastase prefers small neutral residues such as alanine (and glycine) at the P1 position of its substrate.

Elastase is a serine protease that cleaves at the carboxy-terminal of neutral amino acids like alanine and glycine.

Serine proteases are proteolytic enzymes having serine, histidine and aspartate at the active site. The active site consists of two binding sites and a catalytic site. While serine is present in the catalytic site of serine proteases, histidine and aspartate are present on the binding sites.

Serine proteases differ in substrate specificity:

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q001.displayText:
Activation energy is the free-energy gap from substrate to transition state.

Activation energy is the free energy difference between the substrate and the transition state.

Activation energy is defined as the minimum energy required to start a chemical reaction. Because of the high activation energy, the rates of uncatalyzed chemical reactions are often slow. In an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, the activation energy is reduced by forming a relatively stable intermediate enzyme complex. Thus, enzymes increase the rate of chemical reactions.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q002.displayText:
For A + A ⇌ P, the forward elementary rate depends on [A]² and the reverse rate on [P], giving orders 2 and 1.

The above reaction has 2nd order for the forward reaction and 1st order for the reverse reaction.

The sum of the molar ratios of the reactants defines the kinetic order of the reaction.

In the forward reaction, A + A → P, the sum of reactants is 2. Thus, Rate ∝ [A][A], or Rate ∝ [A]². Therefore, the reaction is said to be second order with respect to reactant A.

In the reverse reaction, P → A + A, the sum of reactants is 1. Thus, Rate ∝ [P]. Therefore, the reaction is said to be first order with respect to reactant P.

Kinetic order of reactions:
• Zero-order reaction: Rate is independent of the concentration of reactants.
• First-order reaction: Rate is directly proportional to the concentration of one of the reactants.
• Second-order reaction: In the simplest kind of 2nd order reaction, the rate is proportional to the square of the concentration of one reactant.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q005.displayText:
A Michaelis–Menten velocity-versus-substrate plot is hyperbolic, approaching Vmax as enzyme sites become saturated.

The plot of initial reaction velocity against substrate concentration is hyperbolic, not linear.

For a typical enzyme, the velocity of a reaction has a hyperbolic relationship with the substrate concentration. As the substrate concentration increases, initial velocity (Vi) increases until it reaches a maximum value, Vmax. After Vmax is reached, further increase in the substrate concentration does not change reaction velocity. This is because the enzyme is saturated with the substrate.

The Michaelis constant (Km) is the substrate concentration at which Vi is half the maximal velocity, i.e. Vmax/2. The Michaelis-Menten equation illustrates the relationship between Vi and substrate concentration [S] mathematically, i.e.

Vi = Vmax × [S] / (Km + [S])

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q007.displayText:
At [S] = 1000 Km, velocity is near Vmax; reducing enzyme to one-third makes the same product amount take three times as long.

The time taken for the formation of the same amount of product is 27 minutes.

In this reaction, the substrate concentration is 1000 times the Km value, i.e. much greater than Km. Thus, the rate of the reaction equals Vmax and is independent of the substrate concentration, i.e. it follows zero-order kinetics. Doubling the substrate concentration therefore does not change the velocity of the reaction; it remains at Vmax.

Whatever the substrate concentration, the rate of the reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of the enzyme. Here the enzyme concentration becomes 1/3rd, so the velocity of the reaction (Vmax) also becomes 1/3rd. This means the time taken to form the same amount of product triples, i.e. 9 × 3 = 27 minutes.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q009.displayText:
Competitive inhibition can be overcome at high substrate: Vmax stays the same while apparent Km increases.

Vmax remains constant in competitive inhibition.

In competitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active site of the enzyme. This inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration, by which the maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax (maximum velocity of the reaction) is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the substrate concentration required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q010.displayText:
Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax while leaving Km unchanged; the statement that Km decreases is false.

Km remains constant in noncompetitive inhibition.

Non-competitive inhibition occurs when inhibitors bind to the enzyme at a site different from the active site. The inhibition is not overcome by increasing the substrate concentration. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction.

Non-competitive inhibitors do not resemble the substrate, so they do not interfere with binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the Km of the enzyme does not change. The inhibitor and the substrate bind independently of each other; either or both may be bound at any time, but completing the reaction depends on a conformational change in the enzyme that is blocked by the inhibitor.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q012.displayText:
On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, pure noncompetitive inhibition raises 1/Vmax while preserving Km and therefore the x-intercept.

The red line in the graph represents an enzymatic reaction with a noncompetitive inhibitor.

The above graph is called the 'Lineweaver-Burk plot' or 'double reciprocal' plot. 1/vo (vo = initial velocity) is plotted versus 1/[S] ([S] = substrate concentration) and a straight line is obtained. This plot can be used to calculate Km and Vmax as well as to determine the mechanism of action of enzyme inhibitors. The x-intercept represents -1/Km, while the y-intercept represents 1/Vmax.

In non-competitive inhibition, Vmax decreases (or 1/Vmax increases) but Km is unchanged. Hence the graphs of inhibited and uninhibited reactions have the same x-intercepts (converge at the same -1/Km) but different y-intercepts.

Note: An allosteric inhibitor alters the conformation of an enzyme upon binding. Enzymes affected by allosteric inhibitors exhibit a sigmoid, not hyperbolic, relationship between Vo and [S].

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q013.displayText:
Allosteric modifiers commonly mediate feedback regulation by binding a regulatory site and changing enzyme activity.

An allosteric modifier of an enzyme usually participates in feedback regulation.

Allosteric regulation is a natural example of control loops, such as feedback from downstream products or feedforward from upstream substrates. Allosteric regulation is also particularly important in the cell's ability to adjust enzyme activity.

An allosteric modifier or effector binds to the allosteric site to induce a conformational change in the catalytic or active site. Effectors that enhance the protein's activity are referred to as allosteric activators, whereas those that decrease the protein's activity are called allosteric inhibitors.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q014.displayText:
Allosteric enzymes may show K-type, V-type, or combined effects on apparent substrate affinity and/or Vmax.

Allosterically regulated enzymes belong to either the K-series, the V-series or both.

An allosteric modifier or effector binds to the allosteric site to induce a conformational change in the catalytic or active site. The kinetics of allosteric effectors do not follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Hence, allosterically regulated enzymes fall under the following categories:
• K-series: the allosteric effector raises the Km of the enzyme without affecting Vmax, i.e. similar to competitive inhibition.
• V-series: the allosteric effector lowers the Vmax without affecting Km, i.e. similar to non-competitive inhibition.
• Both: intermediate effects can also be seen.

Option B: An allosteric modifier noncovalently binds to a site other than the active site (allo = other, steric = space) and affects catalysis.

Option C: Induction and repression are methods of controlling the rate of enzyme synthesis, not regulation of activity.

Option D: An allosteric modifier binds to the enzyme noncovalently.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q015.displayText:
Chymotrypsinogen is an inactive zymogen activated by selective proteolytic cleavage to chymotrypsin.

Chymotrypsinogen is a zymogen.

Some enzymes are secreted in an inactive form called zymogens. Zymogens are converted to their active functional forms by partial or selective proteolysis. Examples of zymogens include trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, pepsinogen, prophospholipase A2, etc.

Proenzymes (zymogens) and their active enzymes:
• Pepsinogen → pepsin
• Trypsinogen → trypsin
• Chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin (activated by trypsin)
• Proelastase → elastase (activated by trypsin)
• Procarboxypeptidases → carboxypeptidases (activated by trypsin)

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q016.displayText:
Low-dose aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, a mechanism commonly described as suicide inhibition.

Low dose aspirin exerts its action by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase enzyme activity in platelets, which is an example of suicide inhibition.

A suicidal enzyme is one that undergoes self-destruction in order to terminate its own activity. In this case, in response to irreversible inhibition by aspirin, platelet cyclooxygenase loses its ability to synthesize thromboxane. It undergoes self-destruction. Unless new platelets are formed, this cyclooxygenase activity cannot be regained.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q018.displayText:
Pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km constant and decreases Vmax.

Noncompetitive inhibition has constant Km and decreased Vmax.

Noncompetitive inhibition occurs when the inhibitor binds at a site different from the substrate-binding site. The structure of the inhibitor does not resemble that of the substrate, and the inhibitor does not affect the binding of the substrate.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH19_Q020.displayText:
Compare kcat/Km in common units: option C gives the largest ratio, 200 s⁻¹ / 2 μM = 100 μM⁻¹s⁻¹.

The highest catalytic efficiency is seen when Km = 2 micromole and Kcat = 200 per sec.

Catalytic efficiency is calculated as Kcat/Km, where Km is inversely proportional to the binding affinity of the enzyme and Kcat is the catalytic constant (Vmax divided by the total number of active sites of the enzyme present). Higher values of Kcat and lower values of Km give better catalytic efficiency. Catalytic efficiency can be used to compare the performance of 2 different enzymes in catalyzing a reaction.

Step 1: Km of each option after converting respective units to moles will be 10, 2, 2 and 4 (each multiplied by 10⁻⁶) moles.

Step 2: The catalytic efficiency is calculated as Kcat/Km. On substituting the values in various options after converting to moles, the values come out to be 2, 25, 100 and 50 (each multiplied by 10⁶) M⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Some enzymes can be so efficient that they convert the substrate to product instantaneously. They are limited only by the rate at which substrate diffuses towards the enzyme in a solution. These are called diffusion-limited enzymes, and their catalytic efficiency is as high as 10⁸ M⁻¹ s⁻¹.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q010.displayText:
Vitamin D metabolites act as steroid hormones, regulating calcium/phosphate balance and other cellular functions.

Vitamin D is also considered a hormone.
Vitamin D encompasses a group of sterols, which have a hormone-like function.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH22_Q012.displayText:
Ascorbate reduces dietary ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the more absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺).

Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C.
Vitamin C reduces the ferric iron to its ferrous form, thereby helping in the process of absorption of dietary iron from the intestine.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH24_Q003.displayText:
Purine ring atoms come from glycine, aspartate, glutamine, CO₂ and folate-derived one-carbon units; lysine is not a ring precursor.

Lysine does not contribute to the synthesis of a purine ring.
Glycine, aspartate & glutamine are the amino acids that contribute to synthesizing a purine ring. CO2, N10-Formyl-THFA and N5N10-Methenyl-THFA are the other molecules that influence the structure.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q001.displayText:
Complementary nucleotides on opposite DNA strands pair through hydrogen bonds; each base pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine.

The true statement about DNA is that the nucleotide of one strand binds with the nucleotide of the opposite strand.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymeric molecule containing genetic information. It is a double-stranded molecule consisting of nucleotide pairs. Each nucleotide pair includes one purine and one pyrimidine. The nucleotide of one strand binds with the nucleotide of the opposite strand by hydrogen bonds.

Other options:

Option B: The information from DNA is copied in the form of mRNA.

Option D: Cytosine and uracil differ by one amino group.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q002.displayText:
The marked A–T base-pair interaction is a hydrogen bond; adenine and thymine form two such bonds.

The marked bond represents a hydrogen bond between thymine and adenine.

The complementary nitrogenous bases of the 2 strands of the DNA double helix are linked by hydrogen bonds. Adenine and thymine are linked by two hydrogen bonds (A=T), whereas three hydrogen bonds are present between cytidine and guanine (C≡G). Van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions are present between the stacked adjacent base pairs.

A β-N-glycosidic bond is present between the nitrogenous base and deoxyribose sugar. C1 of deoxyribose/ribose sugar is joined covalently to N1 of pyrimidines and N9 of purines by a β-N-glycosidic bond. An ester bond is present between the sugar and phosphate group of the same nucleotide. An acid anhydride bond is present between two phosphate groups.

A polymer of nucleotides is joined by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds. The bond is present between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate group of another.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q003.displayText:
Chargaff pairing gives A = T = 28%; the remaining 44% is G + C, so cytosine is 22%.

The percentage of cytosine in DNA will be 22%.

According to Chargaff's rule, in cellular DNA, regardless of species:
• A = T and G = C
• Purines = Pyrimidines, i.e. A + G = C + T

In the question it is given that thymine is 28%, therefore adenine is also 28%. So, adenine + thymine = 56% and guanine + cytosine = 44%. Since guanine = cytosine, the percentage of cytosine = 44/2 = 22%.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q005.displayText:
DNA denaturation separates strands without cleaving covalent backbone bonds; unstacked bases absorb more at 260 nm (hyperchromicity).

Hyperchromicity at 260 nm is a feature of denatured DNA.

Denaturation or melting of DNA is a process that separates the two strands into component strands. During denaturation, the hydrogen bonds are broken. The phosphodiester bond is not broken. DNA's secondary and tertiary structures are also broken, but the primary structure is not altered. As DNA gets denatured, its viscosity decreases. Denatured DNA also shows hyperchromicity at 260 nm, which is the increase in absorbance of UV light shown by nitrogenous bases.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q006.displayText:
The nucleosome core octamer contains H2A, H2B, H3 and H4; H1 is the linker histone.

H1 is not a histone found in nucleosomes.

Chromatin is formed by nucleosomes, which are composed of DNA wound around an octameric complex of histone molecules. They contain four major types of histones: H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. Histones are a small family of closely related basic proteins composed of arginine and lysine. H3 and H4 form a tetramer while H2A and H2B form dimers; these histone oligomers associate to form the histone octamer. These four core histones are subject to at least six types of covalent modification or post-translational modification: acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, ADP-ribosylation, monoubiquitylation and sumoylation.

H1 histone is seen in the linker region between nucleosomes and is bound loosely to the nucleosome.

A nucleosome is an octamer of core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4, each one ×2) with core DNA; histone H1 sits on the linker DNA.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q007.displayText:
The (H3–H4)₂ tetramer forms the nucleosome’s central scaffold; H2A–H2B dimers complete the core particle.

The (H3-H4)2 tetramer has a central role in the formation of the nucleosome.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q008.displayText:
Histone H1 phosphorylation, not dephosphorylation, is associated with chromosome condensation during the replication cycle.

Roles of modified histones:
• Phosphorylation of histone H1 is associated with the condensation of chromosomes during the replication cycle.
• Acetylation of H3 and H4 is associated with the activation or inactivation of gene transcription.
• Acetylation of core histones is associated with chromosomal assembly during DNA replication.
• Methylation of histones is correlated with activation and repression of gene transcription.
• ADP-ribosylation of histones is associated with DNA repair.
• Monoubiquitylation is associated with gene activation, repression, and heterochromatic gene silencing.

Methylation and acetylation of histones:
• Methylation of DNA and histones causes nucleosomes to pack tightly together. Transcription factors cannot bind the DNA, and genes are not expressed (DNA inaccessible, gene inactive).
• Histone acetylation results in loose packing of nucleosomes. Transcription factors can bind the DNA and genes are expressed (DNA accessible, gene active).

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q009.displayText:
Heterochromatin is densely packed and stains darkly; it is generally transcriptionally less active and replicates later.

The true statement is that heterochromatin stains densely.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q010.displayText:
The listed chromosome features are all correct: centromeres contain repeats, telomeres have TTAGGG repeats, and each chromatid has one dsDNA molecule.

All of the given statements are correct.

Chromosomes can be visualised during metaphase of mitosis. At this point, they are duplicated with two-fold symmetry. The duplicated, identical sister chromatids are connected at the centromere. Each sister chromatid consists of a single dsDNA molecule. The centromere is an adenine-thymine (A-T) rich region containing repeated DNA sequence. The ends of each chromosome contain structures called telomeres, which have a variable number of repeats of the sequence 5'-TTAGGG-3'. Telomere shortening is associated with aging and malignant transformation.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q011.displayText:
Human mitochondrial DNA contributes about 1% of total cellular DNA and encodes a small set of respiratory-chain proteins and RNAs.

1% of cellular DNA is in mitochondria.

Human mitochondria contain 2 to 10 copies of a small circular ~16 kbp (kilo base pair) dsDNA molecule that makes up approximately 1% of total cellular DNA. Out of 37 genes in human mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), 22 genes code for transfer RNAs, 2 for ribosomal RNAs, and 13 for proteins that play key roles in the respiratory chain. A feature unique to human mitochondrial mtDNA is maternal non-mendelian inheritance, because all mitochondria are contributed by the ovum during zygote formation. Thus, mothers transmit mtDNA to all their offspring.

The mtDNA map shows the control region (d-loop), 12S and 16S rRNA, 22 tRNA-encoding genes and 13 protein-encoding regions, including NADH dehydrogenase, cytochrome b, cytochrome oxidase and ATP synthase subunits.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q012.displayText:
Mitochondrial DNA has a higher mutation rate than nuclear DNA and is inherited maternally; it encodes only a subset of OXPHOS proteins.

The true statement is that mitochondrial DNA has a high mutation rate.

Mitochondrial DNA is circular and double-stranded. It has 16,569 bp (that makes up approximately 1% of total cellular DNA), while nuclear DNA has 3.3 billion bp. It has 37 genes that encode 13 protein subunits of the respiratory chain (out of a total of 67 proteins), i.e. about 20%. It mutates at a rate 5-10 times that of nuclear DNA. Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted by maternal non-mendelian inheritance.

The mtDNA map shows the control region (d-loop), 12S and 16S rRNA, 22 tRNA-encoding genes and 13 protein-encoding regions, including NADH dehydrogenase, cytochrome b, cytochrome oxidase and ATP synthase subunits.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q013.displayText:
The Klenow fragment of DNA polymerase I retains polymerase and 3′→5′ proofreading exonuclease but lacks 5′→3′ exonuclease.

Klenow fragment lacks 5'→3' exonuclease activity.

DNA polymerase I is an enzyme involved in DNA replication. It has polymerase activity along with both 3'→5' and 5'→3' exonuclease activity. When the 5'→3' exonuclease domain is removed, the remaining fragment is called the Klenow fragment. It retains the polymerization and proofreading activities of DNA polymerase I.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q014.displayText:
Genome replication occurs in S phase, the DNA-synthesis interval of the eukaryotic cell cycle.

DNA synthesis occurs in the S phase.

In the cell cycle, replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time, during the synthetic or S phase. During the S phase, mammalian cells contain greater quantities of DNA polymerase than during the nonsynthetic phases of the cell cycle.

The Gap 1 (G1) phase consists of cell growth and preparation for DNA synthesis. It occurs before the S phase. The Gap 2 (G2) phase occurs after the S phase, during which preparation for mitosis (M phase) occurs. Cyclins tightly regulate the transitions between phases of the cell cycle.
• G1: growth
• S: DNA synthesis
• G2: growth and preparation for mitosis
• M: mitosis (cell division)

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q015.displayText:
DNA replication is template-directed, semiconservative, bidirectional and semidiscontinuous; DNA polymerase requires a primer.

DNA replication is not template independent.

DNA replication occurs in the S-phase of the cell cycle. It is semi-conservative, semi-discontinuous and bidirectional. DNA strands separate and each acts as a template strand on which a new complementary strand is synthesized. RNA primer is required. The new strand is always synthesized in the 5'-3' direction and thus, the synthesis of DNA in both strands is not the same.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q016.displayText:
DNA polymerases extend a single-stranded template; the duplex is unwound to expose the template at a replication fork.

In all cells, replication can occur only from a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) template.

Steps of DNA replication:
• Identification of the origins of replication
• ATP hydrolysis-driven unwinding of dsDNA to provide an ssDNA template
• Formation of the replication fork; synthesis of RNA primer
• Initiation of DNA synthesis and elongation
• Formation of replication bubbles with ligation of the newly synthesized DNA segments
• Reconstitution of chromatin structure

The replication fork is formed when DNA helicase unwinds a short segment of the parent dsDNA. Primase initiates the synthesis of an RNA primer. DNA polymerase then initiates DNA synthesis (deoxynucleotide polymerisation) in the 3' to 5' direction. Hence, helicase, primase and polymerases act at the replication fork.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q017.displayText:
Origin-binding initiator protein (DnaA in bacteria) binds the origin and opens the adjacent AT-rich DNA unwinding element.

Ori-binding protein initiates local denaturation and unwinding of DNA during replication.

Splitting of the two DNA strands during replication is initiated when the ori-binding protein (e.g. DnaA protein) binds to the origin of replication (ori). This leads to positive supercoiling of the ori. The adjacent A+T rich region, known as the DNA unwinding element (DUE), undergoes local denaturation and separation. A short region of ssDNA is formed, to which helicases bind and further unwind DNA.

SSB or replication protein-A prevents reannealing of the ssDNA strands generated by helicases. Topoisomerase stabilizes the strain caused during unwinding.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q018.displayText:
Eukaryotic replication protein A binds single-stranded DNA to prevent reannealing and protect it from nucleases.

Replication protein-A prevents strands from reannealing during the process of DNA replication.

Replication protein-A is a type of ssDNA-binding protein (SSB). During DNA replication, it binds to the ssDNA generated by helicases. It shifts the equilibrium between dsDNA and ssDNA in the direction of ssDNA and thus prevents reannealing of strands. It also protects the ssDNA from degradation by nucleases.

Option A: Helicase unwinds the DNA template at the replication fork.

Option B: DNA topoisomerases create a single- or double-stranded break in the helix to add or remove supercoils.

Option D: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond within a strand of double-stranded DNA.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q019.displayText:
Primase synthesizes short RNA primers that provide the 3′-OH required by DNA polymerases.

DNA primase synthesizes RNA primers during replication of DNA.

During DNA replication, DNA is synthesized on a single-stranded DNA template by DNA polymerases in the 5' to 3' direction. However, DNA polymerases require an RNA primer: a short stretch of RNA paired to the DNA template. RNA primers serve as the starting point to which deoxyribonucleotides are added. The RNA in the primers is later replaced by DNA.

Option C: Okazaki fragments are lagging-strand segments built on RNA primers by DNA polymerase δ.

Option D: The leading strand is synthesized by DNA polymerase ε.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q020.displayText:
Prokaryotic DNA polymerase I removes RNA primers with its 5′→3′ exonuclease and fills the resulting gaps with DNA.

The true statement is that DNA polymerase I (pol I) is found in prokaryotes.

The prokaryotic polymerases are DNA polymerases I, II, and III. DNA polymerase I recognizes a "nick" or break in the phosphate backbone, and then removes each RNA primer and fills the gaps with DNA. It does this through its 5'→3' exonuclease activity. It has DNA repair activity through 3'→5' exonuclease activity. DNA polymerase II carries out DNA proofreading and repair. DNA polymerase III is the primary enzyme for the synthesis of the leading strand of DNA.

Option A: DNA polymerase δ (eukaryotic polymerase) synthesizes Okazaki fragments, which are short, newly synthesized DNA fragments that are formed on the lagging template strand during DNA replication. They are complementary to the lagging template strand.

Option C: Primase synthesizes RNA primers to start the replication.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q021.displayText:
DNA polymerase complexes elongate/process and proofread DNA; helicase, not polymerase, unwinds the duplex.

Unwinding of DNA is not a function of the DNA polymerase complex.

A number of different DNA polymerase molecules engage in DNA replication. They share three important properties: chain elongation, processivity, and proofreading. Unwinding of DNA is done by the enzyme helicase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q022.displayText:
Bifunctional alkylating agents can cross-link two DNA bases, producing a two-base lesion within or between strands.

Bifunctional alkylating agent cross-linkage is a type of two-base alteration DNA damage.

Bifunctional alkylating agents, like cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil, are commonly used anti-cancer drugs. They contain two reactive sites and thus can cause intrastrand and interstrand cross-links between two nucleotides.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q023.displayText:
Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) is caused by mismatch-repair defects that allow replication errors to accumulate, especially in microsatellites.

Mismatch repair will be defective in a patient with multiple gastrointestinal polyps and carcinoma, with a positive family history of hereditary non-polyposis colon carcinoma (HNPCC).

Mismatch repair is a DNA repair mechanism that corrects single-nucleotide mismatches, insertions, and deletions introduced by the DNA polymerase during DNA replication.

HNPCC or Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition. It occurs due to defects in DNA mismatch repair genes like MLH1 and MSH2. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability. HNPCC is associated with a high risk of colon cancer. It may also be associated with a risk of developing carcinomas of the endometrium, stomach, small bowel, ovary, pancreas, and transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter and renal pelvis.

The diagnostic criteria for HNPCC are referred to as the Amsterdam criteria or the 3-2-1-0 rule. It includes:
• Three or more relatives with HNPCC-associated cancer (colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer, cancer of the small bowel, ureter, or renal pelvis), one of whom is a first-degree relative of the other two
• At least two successive generations affected
• At least one case diagnosed before age 50 years
• Familial adenomatous polyposis excluded
• Tumors verified by pathologic examination

Other options:

Option B: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum have a defect in the nucleotide excision repair pathway.

Option C: Defect in the base excision repair pathway is seen in patients with MUTYH-associated polyposis.

Option D: Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia are examples of diseases seen in patients with point mutations.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q024.displayText:
UV sensitivity, freckling and early skin cancer indicate xeroderma pigmentosum, caused by defective nucleotide-excision repair of pyrimidine dimers.

Photosensitivity, freckling and skin cancer on the face in a child are suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is an example of defective DNA nucleotide excision repair.

In xeroderma pigmentosum, there is an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure. It is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by exaggerated sunburns and pigmentary changes on exposure to UV radiation. There is an increased risk of non-melanoma and melanoma skin cancers, and of neurodegeneration. Patients are also more prone to smoking-induced lung cancers.

Diagnosis is mainly clinical, and it can be confirmed by cellular tests for defective DNA repair. Management includes sun avoidance and regular follow-up to detect and treat skin cancers. There is no cure for xeroderma pigmentosum.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q025.displayText:
Defective nonhomologous end joining can prevent V(D)J recombination and cause severe combined immunodeficiency.

SCID is associated with defective non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ).

NHEJ is a predominant pathway for DNA double-stranded break repair. NHEJ also functions in class switch recombination, enhancing T and B cell diversity. Thus, NHEJ deficiency leads to combined immunodeficiency due to a failure to carry out recombination efficiently.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is characterised by defects in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses. Genes involved are JAK3, RAG1, and IL-7R. Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including Candida albicans, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Pseudomonas species, cytomegalovirus, varicella, and a host of other bacteria.

X-linked SCID is the most common form, accounting for 50% to 60% of cases; hence, SCID is more common in boys. The genetic defect is a mutation in the common γ-chain (γc) subunit of cytokine receptors. In these patients, the thymus contains lobules of undifferentiated epithelial cells, resembling fetal thymus.

Autosomal recessive SCID is commonly caused by a deficiency of the adenosine deaminase (ADA) enzyme. In these patients, the thymus contains remnants of Hassall's corpuscles.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q026.displayText:
After Cas9 creates a double-strand break, error-prone NHEJ is the common repair route unless a donor template supports homology-directed repair.

Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the major mechanism used by CRISPR-Cas9 for gene repair.

CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) are clustered palindromic sequences found in many bacteria. It is a form of acquired immunity to infection by bacteriophages, which complements the system of restriction endonucleases and methylases. CRISPR uses RNA-based targeting to bring the Cas9 endonuclease to foreign (or any complementary) DNA. Within bacteria, this CRISPR-RNA-Cas9 complex then degrades and inactivates the targeted DNA.

The CRISPR system has been adapted for use in eukaryotic cells for gene deletion, gene editing and even modulation of gene transcription.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q027.displayText:
After transplantation, donor and recipient genomes can coexist in recipient tissues; this genetic chimerism is used to monitor engraftment.

Chimeric DNA is associated with organ transplantation, especially bone-marrow transplantation.

In organ transplantation, chimeric DNA refers to the mixture of donor and recipient genetic material that occurs when donor cells begin functioning within the recipient's body. It is used for long-term monitoring of bone marrow transplant recipients. Detecting changes in the levels of donor-derived cells can provide early warning signs of graft failure, rejection, or relapse of underlying disease.

Note: The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:
• Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)
• Producing proteins such as interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator), insulin, growth hormone and hepatitis B vaccine
• Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations
• Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
• Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
• Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH25_Q028.displayText:
Telomerase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that extends telomeres; it maintains chromosome ends but is not itself a DNA-repair pathway.

The false statement is that telomerase is involved in DNA repair.

Telomeres are the ends of chromosomal DNA. Since prokaryotic DNA is circular, it does not have free ends and hence no telomeres. Thus, telomeres are present only in eukaryotes. Telomeres have TG-rich repeats and usually do not code for any proteins. With every DNA replication during cell division, telomere shortening occurs. Once telomeres are almost negligible or non-existent in length, the DNA is unable to replicate and the cell dies. Hence, there is a limit to the number of times a cell can divide.

In stem cells and cancer cells, an enzyme telomerase having reverse transcriptase activity (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) adds telomeres to the chromosome ends, thereby preserving chromosomal length. It allows the stem cells and cancer cells to multiply many more times than a normal adult cell.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q003.displayText:
RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, so adenine pairs with U in RNA.

Uracil (U) replaces thymine (T) as the complementary base for adenine (A) in RNA.

Difference between RNA and DNA: the nucleobases of RNA (ribonucleic acid) are cytosine, guanine, adenine and uracil, whereas the nucleobases of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) are cytosine, guanine, adenine and thymine.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q008.displayText:
α-Amanitin from death-cap mushrooms strongly inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, blocking mRNA synthesis.

The mushroom death cap (also known as Amanita phalloides) produces the toxin α-amanitin, which inhibits RNA polymerase.

In eukaryotes, α-amanitin forms a tight complex with the polymerase, thereby inhibiting mRNA synthesis and, ultimately, protein synthesis.

Note: Rifampicin inhibits the prokaryotic DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q010.displayText:
The coding (non-template) DNA strand matches the RNA sequence except that DNA has T where RNA has U: 5′-TAAGGC-3′.

The non-template strand or coding strand in the DNA will have the same sequence as the RNA that is produced, except that the non-template or coding strand has T in place of U.

As all sequences are written in the 5' to 3' direction unless otherwise specified, an RNA sequence of UAAGGC would correspond to a DNA sequence, on the non-template strand, of TAAGGC. Both the non-template strand and the RNA produced will be complementary to the template strand. Therefore, the template strand would be ATTCCG (written 5' to 3').

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q011.displayText:
A primary transcript is the initial RNA product synthesized 5′ to 3′ before processing such as capping, splicing or cleavage.

The RNA product, which is synthesized in the 5'-3' direction, is the primary transcript. The primary transcripts are generated by RNA polymerase II.

The longest primary transcript is produced by the dystrophin gene.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q012.displayText:
The 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap promotes RNA processing and translation initiation and protects mRNA from 5′ exonucleases.

7-methylguanosine triphosphate capping of the primary transcript is necessary for:
• Processing of the primary transcript to mRNA
• Translation of the mRNA
• Protection of the mRNA against nucleolytic attack by 5′-exonucleases

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q013.displayText:
Eukaryotic translation initiation factors recognize the 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap to recruit the small ribosomal subunit to mRNA.

The attachment of mRNA to the ribosome is mediated through the guanyl cap at the 5' end.

Eukaryotic mRNAs have 7-methylguanosine caps at the 5' end and poly-A tails at the 3' end.

The 7-methylguanosine caps (guanyl caps) are necessary for:
• Processing of primary transcripts to mRNA
• Mediating the attachment of mRNA to the ribosome for translation
• Protection of mRNA against nucleolytic attack by 5' exonucleases

Other options:

Option A: AAUAAA is present at the 3' end, which is the polyadenylation sequence (poly-A tail). It helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus and aids in translation. After the mRNA enters the cytosol, the poly-A tail is gradually shortened.

Option B: tRNA molecules serve as adapters for the translation of the information in the sequence of nucleotides of the mRNA into specific amino acids.

Option D: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence initiates translation in prokaryotes.

Note: The guanyl cap and poly-A tail aid in attaching the mRNA to the ribosome for translation; however, it is initiated and mediated first through the guanyl cap. The poly(A) tail stimulates recruitment of the 40S ribosomal subunit to the mRNA, after which the ribosomal subunit binds to the guanyl cap at the 5' end of mRNA.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q015.displayText:
tRNA does not undergo conventional 5′ cap addition; mRNA and several small regulatory/noncoding RNAs are capped or otherwise processed.

tRNA of alanine does not require 5' capping.

The capping process protects the 5' end of mRNA from the action of exonucleases, and polyadenylation protects the 3' end of the mRNA. All mRNA, snRNA, and siRNA undergo this process, but tRNAs are comparatively stable and do not require capping at the 5' end.

Note: rRNAs also do not require 5' capping.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q016.displayText:
Self-splicing introns catalyze their own removal through RNA folding and transesterification without a spliceosome protein catalyst.

Self-splicing introns do not require a spliceosome or any other proteins for the splicing reaction.

Self-splicing introns fold into complex loops and undergo transesterification reactions, thus undergoing self-splicing.

Other options:

Option A: Split genes have the advantage that they allow alternative splicing, so that a single gene can code for variant forms of the same protein.

Option C: β-thalassemia results from the faulty splicing of the β-globin transcript. However, the spliceosome is normal and the reason for the fault is a mutation in the β-globin gene itself.

Option D: Splicing occurs in the nucleus, and mature transcripts are then transported into the cytosol for translation (protein synthesis) to occur.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q017.displayText:
RNA editing changes transcript sequence; the source example inserts uridines in a 3′-to-5′ editing process, unlike 5′-to-3′ polymer synthesis.

RNA editing occurs in the 3' to 5' direction. It is the process by which the coding sequence is changed at the mRNA level before translation.

RNA editing occurs by insertion of additional Us at the 3' end of the mRNA and proceeds in a 3' to 5' direction. The guide RNA (gRNA) acts as a template for the editing process.

An example of RNA editing is the apoB gene and mRNA. In the intestine, RNA editing changes a CAA codon to UAA, causing a STOP instead of Gln, so the mRNA is translated to apolipoprotein B48. In the liver there is no RNA editing, and the mRNA is translated to apolipoprotein B100.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q018.displayText:
eIF4 complex (including cap-binding eIF4E) recognizes the mRNA 5′ cap during eukaryotic initiation.

The eukaryotic initiation factor (eIF) that helps in cap binding is eIF4.

eIFs are accessory proteins that help initiate protein synthesis.

Functions of eIF:
• eIF3 and eIF1A: The first step of initiation involves dissociation of the ribosome into its 40S and 60S subunits. eIF3 and eIF1A bind to the newly dissociated 40S ribosomal subunit and hence delay the association of 40S and 60S.
• eIF2: It is involved in the formation of a binary complex (GTP-eIF2). This complex binds to met-tRNAi. Further, the GTP-eIF2-tRNAi ternary complex binds to the 40S ribosomal subunit to form the 43S preinitiation complex. This is the second step of initiation.
• eIF4: It forms the cap binding complex. It binds to the 5' terminal of mRNA molecules which are capped. The mRNA then binds to the 43S preinitiation complex to form the 48S initiation complex, in the third step of initiation.
• eIF5: It is involved in the hydrolysis of GTP bound to eIF2. This results in binding of the 60S subunit with the 48S initiation complex to form the 80S initiation complex. This is the fourth step of initiation.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q020.displayText:
Pyrrolysine is the 22nd genetically encoded amino acid and can be inserted at UAG in specific organisms; selenocysteine is the 21st at UGA.

Pyrrolysine is coded by UAG is the correct statement.

Other options:

Option A: Selenocysteine is coded by UGA and not UAA.

Option C: Selenocysteine is considered the 21st amino acid.

Option D: Other names of stop codons are as follows:
• UAA: Ochre
• UAG: Amber
• UGA: Opal

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q021.displayText:
Apolipoprotein B48 is produced in intestine by C-to-U RNA editing that creates a premature stop codon in APOB mRNA.

The process of apolipoprotein B48 synthesis involves RNA editing.

RNA editing is the process by which the coding sequence of the mRNA is changed before translation. As a result, the mRNA template differs from the DNA from which it was transcribed. This leads to the formation of a different protein. This occurs by insertion of additional uracils at the 3' end of the mRNA and proceeds in the 3' to 5' direction.

RNA editing in apoB synthesis:
• In the liver, the apoB gene is transcribed to mRNA, which is then translated to apoB100.
• In the intestine, the same apoB gene is transcribed to the same mRNA. But now, the mRNA undergoes editing by the enzyme cytidine deaminase, which converts the CAA codon in the mRNA to UAA at a single specific site. This edited mRNA translates to apoB48.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH26_Q022.displayText:
The illustrated exon/promoter arrangement yields product A from promoters W and Y, which direct transcription of the included segments.

Among the given options, using promoters W and Y will yield the desired product A.

Promoters or DNA regulatory elements usually precede the desired exon to be transcribed. They help direct transcription of only the desired exons of a gene to yield a product. Alternative splicing utilizes different promoters to code slightly different products from the same gene.

In this question, the desired product A has segments 1, 3, 4 and 5, whilst the other product B has 1, 2, 4 and 5. The difference between both is the presence of segment 3 in product A and the presence of segment 2 in product B. As the product in question is A, only segment 3 is required, while excluding segment 2 and keeping segments 1, 4 and 5 intact.
• Segment 1: Needs to be transcribed, so W is essential.
• Segment 2: Does not need to be transcribed.
• Segment 3: Needs to be transcribed, so Y is essential.
• Segment 4: Needs to be transcribed, but Z is not essential as Y continues the transcription in the direction shown by the arrow.

The answer is hence promoters W and Y.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q001.displayText:
Restriction endonucleases recognize specific DNA sequences and cleave the DNA internally at or near those sites.

Enzymes that cut DNA at specific DNA sequences within the molecule are called restriction enzymes.

These defensive enzymes protect the host bacterial DNA from the genomes of foreign organisms (primarily infective phages) by specifically inactivating the invading phage DNA by digestion.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q002.displayText:
Restriction endonucleases are paired with cognate DNA methylases that mark host sites and protect them from self-digestion.

Restriction enzymes are found with site-specific DNA methylases.

Restriction endonucleases are present in cells that also have a companion enzyme that site-specifically methylates the host DNA, thus rendering it an unsuitable substrate for digestion by that particular restriction enzyme.

Thus, site-specific DNA methylases and restriction enzymes that target the same sites always exist in pairs in a bacterium.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q006.displayText:
The source identifies bacteriophages as vectors with linear DNA; plasmids and cosmids are generally circular constructs.

Phages have linear DNA into which foreign DNA can be inserted at several restriction enzyme sites.

Amplification of DNA (cloning) is done using cloning vectors: bacterial plasmids, phages, or cosmids.

Bacterial plasmids are small, circular, duplex DNA molecules whose natural function is to confer antibiotic resistance on the host cell. A cosmid is a plasmid into which DNA sequences from bacteriophage lambda (λ cos sites) have been inserted. This enables packaging of the plasmid DNA in vitro. Cosmids have small, circular, duplex DNA. (Options B and C)
