marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q007.displayText:
A genomic library is a collection of recombinant clones representing most of an organism's genomic DNA, including coding and noncoding regions.

A genomic library is bacteria with plasmids containing DNA fragments representing the majority of the genetic information from a plant or animal.

The combination of restriction enzymes and various cloning vectors allows the entire genome of an organism to be individually packed into vectors. A collection of these different recombinant clones is called a library.

A genomic library is prepared from the total DNA of a cell line or tissue. A cDNA library comprises complementary DNA copies of the population of mRNAs in a tissue. (Option C)

Genomic DNA libraries are often prepared by partial digestion of total DNA with a restriction enzyme that cuts DNA frequently.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q008.displayText:
Northern blotting detects RNA; Southern blotting detects DNA and Western blotting detects proteins.

Northern blotting is used for the detection of RNA.

Southern blotting is used for the detection of DNA, and Western blotting is used for the detection of protein.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q010.displayText:
Ideal PCR doubles target DNA each cycle; 30 cycles yield about 2³⁰, or 10⁹, copies from one template.

A PCR reaction that continues for 30 cycles will produce approximately 1 billion PCR products from a single template DNA molecule.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a method of amplifying a target sequence of DNA. DNA sequences as short as 50 to 100 bp and as long as 10 kb can be amplified by PCR. The amplification is exponential.
• 20 cycles provide an amplification of 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, or 1 million copies
• 30 cycles provide an amplification of 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹, or 1 billion copies

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q011.displayText:
PCR needs template, primers, ordinary dNTPs and thermostable DNA polymerase; ddNTPs terminate chains and are used in sequencing.

Dideoxy-dNTPs (ddNTPs) are not required in a PCR reaction.

In a PCR reaction, the DNA sample is first heat-denatured (>90°C) to separate the two strands of the template DNA containing the target sequence. The primers, added in excess, are allowed to anneal to the DNA (typically 50-75°C), and each strand is copied by a DNA polymerase, starting at the primer sites, in the presence of all four dNTPs (again in vast excess).

DNA synthesis is catalyzed by a heat-stable DNA polymerase purified from one of a number of different thermophilic bacteria, organisms that grow at 70-80°C.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q012.displayText:
PCR can detect infectious agents, support prenatal genotyping and reveal allelic polymorphisms, so all listed uses apply.

All of the listed options are applications of PCR.

The applications of PCR to forensic medicine are as follows:
• To detect infectious agents, especially latent viruses
• Make prenatal genetic diagnoses
• Detect allelic polymorphisms
• Establish precise tissue types for transplants
• To study evolution, using DNA from archeological samples
• For quantitative RNA analyses after RNA copying and mRNA quantitation by the so-called RT-PCR method (cDNA copies of mRNA generated by a retroviral reverse transcriptase)
• To score in vivo protein-DNA occupancy using chromatin immunoprecipitation assays

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q013.displayText:
RT-PCR reverse-transcribes RNA to cDNA and amplifies it, enabling measurement or detection of transcript expression.

RT-PCR is a method that is used for analysis of mRNA expression and its amplification.

Reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is a variant of PCR and includes 2 steps:
• Generation of complementary DNA (cDNA copies) from mRNA using reverse transcriptase, used to qualitatively detect gene expression
• Amplification of the newly synthesized cDNA by traditional PCR. This can be quantitatively measured by using fluorescent dyes (qRT-PCR).

Uses:
• Determination of viral load in disease
• Screening of genetic diseases and cancers

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q016.displayText:
Sickle-cell disease results from a single nucleotide substitution in HBB that changes β-globin Glu6 to Val.

Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation.

This is caused by mutation of a single base out of the 3 × 10⁹ in the genome, a T-to-A DNA substitution, resulting in an A-to-U change in the mRNA corresponding to the sixth codon of the β-globin gene.

Defective production of β-globin results in a variety of diseases and is due to many different lesions in and around the β-globin gene.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q017.displayText:
RFLPs can support linkage mapping, QTL mapping and diagnosis of single-gene variants when a polymorphism tracks the disease allele.

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is used to construct high-resolution linkage maps and QTL maps, and to identify single-gene diseases.

An inherited difference in the pattern of restriction enzyme digestion (e.g. a DNA variation occurring in more than 1% of the general population) is known as a restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP). RFLPs result from single-base changes (e.g. sickle-cell disease) or from deletions or insertions (CNVs) of DNA in a restriction fragment (e.g. the thalassemias), and have proved to be useful diagnostic tools.

SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) and RFLPs can be used to establish linkage groups, which in turn, by the process of chromosome walking, eventually define the disease locus.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q019.displayText:
GATATC is palindromic (its reverse complement is GATATC) and is recognized by restriction enzymes such as EcoRV.

Restriction endonuclease enzymes act at specific palindromic sequences that create DNA fragments of different lengths. By analyzing the fragments, specific species of bacteria can be identified. Option B is the only palindromic sequence here, hence it is the answer.

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis is a technique that involves cutting a particular region of DNA with known variability with restriction enzymes, then separating the DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis and determining the number of fragments and their relative sizes.

Cleavage of a sample of DNA with a restriction enzyme produces a characteristic set of smaller DNA fragments. Deviations in the normal product pattern produce RFLPs, which occur if a mutation renders a restriction site unrecognizable or alternatively generates a new recognition site.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q020.displayText:
Tandem mass spectrometry profiles amino acids, acylcarnitines and other metabolites in newborn screening for inherited metabolic disorders.

Tandem mass spectrometry (MS) is the technique of choice for screening neonates for inherited metabolic diseases.

Tandem MS employs the equivalent of two mass spectrometers linked in series (MS-MS or MS2). It can be used to screen blood samples from newborns for the presence and concentrations of amino acids, fatty acids, and other metabolites.

Abnormalities in metabolite levels indicate inherited metabolic diseases, such as phenylketonuria, ethylmalonic encephalopathy, and glutaric acidemia type 1.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q021.displayText:
Ion-exchange chromatography separates hemoglobin fractions by charge and is a standard method for HbA1c measurement.

The best method to measure HbA1c is ion-exchange chromatography.

In ion-exchange chromatography:
• Proteins interact with the stationary phase by charge-charge interactions.
• Proteins with a net positive charge at a given pH adhere tightly to beads with negatively charged functional groups such as carboxylates or sulfates (cation exchangers).
• Proteins with a net negative charge adhere to beads with positively charged functional groups, typically tertiary or quaternary amines (anion exchangers).
• Non-adherent proteins flow through the matrix and are washed away.
• Proteins elute in inverse order of the strength of their interactions with the stationary phase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q022.displayText:
Blue-white screening uses α-complementation of β-galactosidase: an inserted DNA fragment disrupts lacZα and changes colony color.

The image shows a schematic representation of the blue-white assay used in the screening of recombinant vectors for inserted DNA fragments. It uses the phenomenon of complementation (alpha-complementation of the β-galactosidase gene).

Blue-white assay: The DNA of interest is ligated into a vector. The vector is then inserted into a competent host cell viable for transformation, which is then grown in the presence of X-gal (X-gal detects active β-galactosidase). Cells transformed with vectors containing recombinant DNA will produce white colonies, whereas cells transformed with non-recombinant plasmids (i.e. only the vector) grow into blue colonies.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q023.displayText:
Spectral karyotyping (SKY), a multicolor FISH method, identifies chromosomal translocations such as t(9;22) in CML.

Translocation in the Philadelphia chromosome (a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22) is best studied by SKY.

SKY stands for spectral karyotyping or multicolor FISH (M-FISH). This technique allows one to display all the chromosomes together and thus helps identify chromosomal defects in conditions such as chronic myeloid leukemia.

Other options:

Option A: G banding is also a karyotyping technique, but SKY is the better option of the two.

Option C: Southern blotting is a technique used to detect a specific DNA sequence in a tissue sample.

Option D: DNA sequencing cannot detect a structural abnormality in a chromosome.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q024.displayText:
DNA microarrays use hybridization to detect known sequence variants and compare gene-expression patterns across many probes.

DNA microarray can be used to detect DNA sequence variations.

There are various microarray techniques used in clinical practice, which are described below.

DNA microarray technique or DNA chip:
• Fluorescent-labelled unknown oligonucleotide is added to the DNA chip containing known oligonucleotide sequences.
• Computerised algorithms can decode the unknown oligonucleotide by detecting the location of the fluorescent hybridization pattern on the chip.
• This technique is used for genotyping or genome sequencing.

RNA microarray: RNA microarray can detect gene expression.
• Fluorescently labelled cDNA prepared from unknown mRNA is added to the known array of oligonucleotides, and the unknown cDNA is decoded.
• This technique is used for gene expression studies.

Protein microarray:
• Known antibodies are placed on a glass slide and fluorescently tagged target protein is added. The target protein is detected by antigen-antibody interaction.
• This technique is used in the study of proteomics.

In a microarray, fully complementary strands bind strongly to the fixed probes, while partially complementary strands bind weakly.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q025.displayText:
Array comparative genomic hybridization detects copy-number changes but cannot detect balanced rearrangements without net DNA gain or loss.

Array CGH cannot detect balanced translocation.

In array-based CGH, two genomes are compared. The test DNA and the reference DNA are labelled with two different fluorescent dyes (red and green respectively) and are added to a DNA chip spotted with the entire human genome.
• If the contributions of both samples are equal for a given chromosomal region, then all spots on the array will fluoresce yellow.
• If the test sample has an amplification, that spot will fluoresce red.
• If the test sample has a deletion, that spot will fluoresce green.

Uses of array CGH:
• To detect gene amplification
• To detect gene deletion
• To detect copy number variations

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q026.displayText:
PCR cycles through denaturation, primer annealing and extension to amplify the target DNA.

The correct sequence of events for PCR among the given options is denaturation, annealing, and extension.

The process of PCR is as follows:
The DNA sample is first heat-denatured at >90°C (90-96°C for 3 minutes) to separate the two strands of the template DNA containing the target sequence. The primers (which attach to the 3' end of the flanking sequence) are added in excess and are allowed to anneal to the DNA (typically at 50-75°C) in order to generate the required template-primer hybridization complex. Under suitable conditions and in the presence of deoxynucleotides, elongation of the DNA strand occurs.

The number of copies produced in the presence of an unlimited supply of deoxynucleotides and enzymes is given by 2 to the power n (where n is the number of PCR cycles).
• 20 cycles provide an amplification of 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, or 1 million copies.
• 30 cycles provide an amplification of 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹, or 1 billion copies.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH28_Q027.displayText:
Wobble at the third codon position lets one tRNA recognize multiple synonymous codons, explaining genetic-code degeneracy.

The wobble hypothesis explains the degeneracy of the genetic code.

The wobble hypothesis states that codon-anticodon pairing follows the traditional Watson-Crick rules (G pairs with C and A pairs with U) for the first two bases of the codon but can be less stringent for the third/last base. It has been observed that a tRNA can recognize more than one codon for a specific amino acid, especially in the last nucleotide of the codon triplet. This is referred to as degeneracy, and its mechanism can be explained by the wobble hypothesis.

The first base of the anticodon moves to permit nontraditional pairing with the last base of the codon. This movement is called wobble and is possible because the first base of the anticodon is not as spatially defined as the other two bases. Due to the wobbling, 61 tRNA species are not required to read the 61 codons.

For example, three codons for glycine (GGU, GGC, and GGA) can form a base pair with one anticodon, 3' CCI 5', i.e. I (inosine) can base pair with U, C, and A.

Other options:

Option A: The genetic code is universal because it is the same for all living organisms.

Option B: The genetic code is unambiguous because each codon is specific for only one amino acid. Example: GGA only codes for glycine.

Option D: The genetic code is non-punctuated. This means that once the reading commences at a specific start codon, it is read continuously as triplets until a stop codon is reached.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q021.displayText:
Hering-Breuer reflexes are mediated by slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors, and the impulses travel in the vagus nerve via large myelinated fibers.

Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: "Prolonged inspiration inhibits further inspiration."
• Hyperinflation of the lungs stimulates slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors, and the impulses travel in the vagus nerve via large myelinated fibers.
• This signal inhibits the inspiratory ramp signals of the dorsal respiratory group of neurons (DRG), thus, inspiration is quickly inhibited and expiration follows.
• Advantages of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: it cuts down the inspiration time and, therefore, prevents overinflation of the lungs. The lungs operate at lower lung volumes, thereby preventing wastage of energy.
• The Hering-Breuer reflex is activated when the lung volume increases to more than three times the normal tidal volume (tidal volume = 0.5 liters/breath; so a lung volume > 1.5 liters per breath activates the reflex).
• It signifies that the reflex plays a protective role, preventing overinflation of the lung, rather than regulating normal ventilation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q028.displayText:
Respiratory rhythm generation is a function of the dorsal respiratory group of neurons (and not the pneumotaxic center).

Pneumotaxic center:
• It is located dorsally in the nucleus parabrachialis of the upper pons, and it transmits signals to the inspiratory area.
• The primary effect of this center is to control the switch-off point of the inspiratory ramp, thus controlling the duration of the filling phase of the lung cycle.
• The function of the pneumotaxic center is primarily to limit inspiration, which has a secondary effect of increasing the rate of breathing, because limitation of inspiration also shortens expiration and the entire period of each respiration.
emphasis: controlling the duration of the filling phase of the lung cycle.
the entire period of each respiration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH26_Q018.displayText:
Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation.

The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein. From the umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava. From here, the blood enters the heart via the right atrium. The right atrium also receives deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava. This mixed blood is distributed to the body via the aorta.

Therefore, the inferior vena cava has the highest concentration of oxygen in the fetal circulation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q001.displayText:
Severe cerebral ischemia strongly activates medullary vasomotor centers, making the CNS ischemic response the most powerful sympathetic activator.

The most powerful activator of the sympathetic vasomotor system is the CNS ischemic response.

CNS ischemic response:
When blood flow to the vasomotor center in the lower brainstem (medulla) is severely decreased, the local concentration of CO₂ increases greatly and has a potent effect in stimulating the sympathetic vasomotor control areas in the medulla. Blood pressure may rise to 250 mmHg. The strong activation may cause some peripheral vessels to occlude.

It does not activate until arterial pressure drops to 60 mmHg or less; hence it is principally an emergency mechanism.

Note: Baroreceptors are the most common activators, but not the most powerful.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q003.displayText:
Recumbency increases venous return; in left-sided heart failure, the pulmonary veins act as a reservoir and congestion worsens orthopnea.

The given scenario describes orthopnea in congestive heart failure. It is due to the reservoir function of the pulmonary veins.

Orthopnea is dyspnea occurring in the recumbent position.

It results from redistribution of fluid from the splanchnic circulation and lower extremities (increased venous return) into the heart during recumbency. This increased venous return is not put out by the failing left ventricle and hence pools in the pulmonary veins, which act as capacitance vessels (reservoir function), adding to the already congested pulmonary vasculature and resulting in breathing difficulty.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q004.displayText:
Lung interstitial pressure is slightly negative; encapsulated organs and rigid closed compartments can have positive pressure.

The interstitial fluid pressure is negative in the lungs.

The interstitial fluid pressure is slightly negative in the body except in the encapsulated organs.

It is positive in:
• Rigid closed compartments: bone marrow, brain
• Encapsulated organs: kidney, skeletal muscle

This is because, in the kidney, high-pressure vessels push the interstitial fluid against an unyielding fibrous capsule, raising the pressure. The same principle applies to skeletal muscle surrounded by layers of fascia.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q006.displayText:
An acute transfusion reaction can cause distributive shock through mediator-driven systemic vasodilation and reduced vascular resistance.

The shock due to a transfusion reaction is distributive shock.

During a transfusion reaction, there is decreased systemic vascular resistance due to system-wide vasodilation mediated by release of histamine by mast cells in response to antigen-bound IgE, leading to distributive shock.

Types of circulatory shock:
• Hypovolemic shock: due to decreased blood in the vascular compartment, e.g. haemorrhage, dehydration.
• Cardiogenic shock: due to decreased capacity of the heart to pump, e.g. any pathology of the heart decreasing its ability to maintain cardiac output.
• Obstructive shock: due to conditions causing obstruction to blood flow in the lungs and heart, e.g. pulmonary embolism.
• Distributive/vasculogenic shock: excessive vasodilation leading to impaired organ perfusion, e.g. septic shock, SIRS, transfusion reaction, Addisonian crisis, neurogenic shock.

Three stages of shock:
• Non-progressive: also called compensated shock, where the normal compensatory mechanisms eventually cause full recovery without help from outside therapy.
• Progressive: also called decompensated shock; without therapy, it gets steadily worse.
• Irreversible: even therapy is inadequate to save life.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q010.displayText:
Septic shock can have high cardiac output because systemic vasodilation lowers resistance while metabolic demand rises.

Septic shock is characterized by high cardiac output.

High cardiac output in septic shock is caused by:
• Arteriolar dilation in the infected tissues
• High metabolic rate and vasodilation (resulting from bacterial toxins stimulating cellular metabolism and from high body temperature)

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q015.displayText:
Carotid baroreceptor afferents travel in Hering’s nerve and glossopharyngeal nerve to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla.

The Hering's nerve terminates in the medulla (tractus solitarius).

Baroreceptor reflexes:
• Carotid baroreceptors → Hering's nerve → glossopharyngeal nerve → tractus solitarius in the medulla
• Aortic baroreceptors → vagus nerve → tractus solitarius in the medulla

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q017.displayText:
Mayer waves are slow arterial-pressure oscillations generated by delayed reflex changes in neural blood-pressure control.

Mayer waves are due to the variation of arterial pressure caused by reflex changes in the nervous control of blood pressure.

The most important mechanisms are as follows:

I. Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflex: high pressure excites the baroreceptors → inhibits the sympathetic nervous system and lowers the pressure → the decreased pressure, in turn, reduces the baroreceptor stimulation → elevating the pressure to a high value (the response is not instantaneous; it is delayed until a few seconds later). This high pressure then initiates another cycle, and the oscillation continues.

II. Oscillation of the CNS ischemic response: the cerebrospinal fluid pressure is raised to 160 mm Hg → causes compression of cerebral blood vessels → cerebral ischemia → the CNS ischemic pressure response raises the arterial pressure up to 200 mm Hg → the brain ischemia is relieved and the sympathetic nervous system becomes inactive → the arterial pressure falls rapidly back to a much lower value, causing brain ischemia once again → initiates another rise in pressure. This chain of events repeats itself cyclically as long as the cerebrospinal fluid pressure remains elevated.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q002.displayText:
Cardiac output is measured by Fick principle, thermodilution or imaging; V/Q ratio assesses pulmonary ventilation-perfusion matching.

The V/Q ratio is not used to determine cardiac output.

Measurement of cardiac output:
• Fick principle
• Dye dilution/thermodilution
• Doppler plus echocardiography
• MRI

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q003.displayText:
Cardiac output divided by heart rate gives stroke volume per beat.

Cardiac output in litres per minute divided by heart rate gives stroke volume.

Cardiac output = Heart rate × Stroke volume.

The stroke volume, the amount of blood pumped out of each ventricle per beat, is about 70 mL from each ventricle in a resting man in the supine position.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q007.displayText:
Frank–Starling law links greater venous return and end-diastolic filling to stronger contraction and higher stroke volume/output.

Starling's law implies that increased venous return leads to increased cardiac output.

Frank-Starling law: the energy of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fibre.

The length of the muscle fibres is proportional to the end-diastolic volume, which is determined by venous return.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q008.displayText:
Gravity raises dependent arterial pressure but does not aid venous return; valves, muscle pump and fascia support return while standing.

Venous return to the heart during quiet standing is not facilitated by increased arterial pressure.

Factors that facilitate venous return to the heart:
• Calf muscles contract and pump blood through the veins.
• Valves do not allow retrograde flow of blood through the veins.
• Deep fascia forms a supporting structure for the veins.

Note: Arterial pulsations help increase lymph flow.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q010.displayText:
Stroke volume is 120−50=70 mL; at 70 beats/min cardiac output is 4,900 mL/min.

When a person changes position from standing to supine, venous return to the heart rises immediately. On standing, gravitational pull causes venous pooling of blood in the legs. In the supine position, this gravitational pull equalizes over the body, causing the pooled blood to return back to the heart.

Other options:

Option A: Heart rate decreases because of increased cardiac output and increased BP via the baroreceptor reflex.

Option C: Cerebral blood flow will remain constant due to autoregulation.

Option D: Blood flow to the apex of the lung will be high due to high cardiac output.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q013.displayText:
Isovolumetric relaxation ends when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure and the AV valve opens.

The end of the isovolumetric relaxation phase is indicated when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.

Events of the cardiac cycle:

Diastole:
• Protodiastole: Before the semilunar valve closes, even though the ventricular muscle is relaxed, blood flow into the great vessels continues due to the momentum of blood.
• Isovolumetric relaxation: The ventricular muscle continues to relax, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.
• Ventricular filling: Isovolumetric relaxation ends when the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure and the AV valves open, permitting the ventricles to fill.
• Atrial systole: During the last third of diastole, the atria contract and give additional thrust to the inflow of blood into the ventricles. It correlates with the 'a' wave in the JVP.

Systole:
• Isovolumetric contraction: The ventricular muscle continues to contract, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed. It correlates with the 'c' wave of the JVP.
• Ventricular ejection: When the ventricular pressures rise above the aortic and pulmonary pressures, the valves open and ventricular ejection begins. Peak pressures in the left and right ventricles are about 120 and 25 mmHg, respectively.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q014.displayText:
The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure at the end of isovolumetric contraction.

Opening of the aortic valve takes place at the end of isovolumetric contraction.

When the ventricular pressures rise above the aortic and pulmonary pressures, the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary valves) open, and ventricular ejection begins.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q017.displayText:
Mitral stenosis reduces LV filling and shifts the pressure-volume loop leftward with reduced end-diastolic volume.

The pressure-volume curve is shifted to the left in mitral stenosis.

The PV loop is shifted to the right when there is volume overload (increased EDV).

The PV loop is shifted to the left in case of increased contractility or decreased compliance (decreased EDV).

Effect of valvular diseases on the PV loop:
• Mitral stenosis: Left and down.
• Mitral regurgitation: Width increased and height decreased.
• Aortic stenosis: Tall with steep slope.
• Aortic regurgitation: Right and tall.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q018.displayText:
The dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure trace follows aortic valve closure and brief elastic recoil.

Dicrotic notch is caused by closing of the aortic valve.

The dicrotic notch is a small oscillation in the falling phase of the pulse wave, caused by vibrations set up when the aortic valve shuts.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q019.displayText:
S1 is AV-valve closure; S2 is semilunar-valve closure.

The first heart sound and the second heart sound are due to closure of the atrioventricular (AV) and semilunar valves respectively.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q020.displayText:
S4 is a late-diastolic sound from atrial contraction forcing blood into a stiff ventricle.

The fourth heart sound is caused by ventricular filling.

A fourth sound is heard immediately before the first sound when atrial pressure is high or the ventricle is stiff, as in ventricular hypertrophy. It is due to ventricular filling and is rarely heard in normal adults.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q021.displayText:
The JVP a wave is caused by right atrial contraction.

The 'a' wave in the JVP represents atrial contraction.

Waves of the JVP:
• a: atrial systole pushing the blood into the ventricles.
• c: isovolumetric contraction of the ventricles, causing the tricuspid valve to bulge.
• x: fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole due to the pull of the valve leaflets.
• v: venous filling, which creates an increase in atrial pressure.
• y: passive filling of the ventricles by passive flow of blood from the right atrium.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q022.displayText:
The JVP c wave occurs during isovolumetric ventricular contraction as the tricuspid valve bulges into the atrium.

'c' waves are produced by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during the isovolumetric contraction of the right ventricle.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q023.displayText:
The JVP x descent occurs during ventricular systole as atrial relaxation and downward tricuspid displacement lower right atrial pressure.

• a wave: corresponds to right atrial contraction.
• c wave: corresponds to bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
• x descent: corresponds to atrial relaxation as ventricular systole pulls the tricuspid valve down during ejection.
• v wave: corresponds to venous filling of the right atrium against a closed tricuspid valve.
• y descent: corresponds to the fall in right atrial pressure during passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q024.displayText:
The JVP c wave reflects the tricuspid valve bulging into the right atrium during isovolumetric contraction.

The 'c' wave in the JVP represents the tricuspid bulge into the right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

Characteristics of the JVP:
• The a wave corresponds to atrial systole, which causes regurgitation of blood into the great veins.
• The c wave occurs due to the increase in atrial pressure caused by bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
• The x descent occurs due to the fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole, due to pulling of the valve leaflets.
• The v wave is seen at the end of ventricular ejection and occurs due to the slow venous filling, which causes an increase in atrial pressure.
• The y descent occurs due to the passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q025.displayText:
The Bainbridge reflex raises heart rate when increased venous return distends the right atrium.

The reflex responsible for tachycardia during right atrial distension is the Bainbridge reflex.

Atrial reflex control of heart rate (the Bainbridge reflex):
• The stretch receptors of the atria that elicit the Bainbridge reflex transmit their afferent signals through the vagus nerves to the medulla.
• Efferent signals are then transmitted back through vagal and sympathetic nerves to increase the heart rate and the strength of contraction.

Bezold-Jarisch reflex:
• Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibres in the cardiopulmonary region (e.g. the juxtacapillary region of the alveoli, ventricles, atria, great veins, and pulmonary artery) causes profound bradycardia, hypotension and a brief period of apnea followed by rapid shallow breathing.

Cushing reflex:
• When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to the RVLM neurons is compromised.
• The local hypoxia and hypercapnia increase the discharge from these neurons, producing hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.
• The resulting rise in systemic arterial pressure tends to restore the blood flow to the medulla.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q026.displayText:
After the P wave, atrial contraction precedes AV conduction delay, ventricular depolarization and ventricular systole; the printed sequence is 1–2–4–3.

The correct sequence of events that occur after the P wave is 1-2-4-3, i.e. a wave in JVP → first heart sound → T wave in ECG → rapid filling of the ventricles.
• The P wave in the ECG represents atrial depolarization, which causes contraction of the atria, represented by the 'a' wave in the JVP. Atrial contraction causes the final filling of the ventricles.
• Atrial contraction is followed by closure of the mitral valve, which causes the first heart sound.
• This is followed by isovolumetric contraction of the ventricle, which causes the c wave in the JVP due to bulging of the tricuspid valve, and then by the rapid ejection phase.
• The T wave of the ECG occurs during ventricular repolarization. It is followed by opening of the mitral valve and then the rapid filling phase of the ventricle.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q027.displayText:
Pregnancy raises cardiac output through increased blood volume, heart rate and stroke volume.

Cardiac output is increased in pregnancy.

Effect of various conditions on cardiac output:

displayTables.title: Effect of various conditions on cardiac output
rows: Sleep; moderate changes in environmental temperature
Anxiety and excitement; eating; exercise; high environmental temperature; pregnancy; epinephrine
Sitting or standing from lying position; rapid arrhythmias; heart disease

marrow__PHYSIO_CH29_Q001.displayText:
The SA node is the normal pacemaker because it has the fastest spontaneous phase-4 depolarization and intrinsic firing rate.

The SA node acts as the pacemaker of the heart because it generates impulses at the highest rate (60-100/min), compared with the AV node (40-60/min) and the Purkinje fibres (15-40/min). The impulses generated by the SA node are conducted through the AV node and the Purkinje fibres so repeatedly that these never reach their own thresholds for self-excitation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q014.displayText:
Jejunal resection most threatens major fluid/electrolyte absorption because it removes a large area of small-intestinal absorptive surface.

The resection of jejunum leads to major electrolyte imbalance because most of the fluid and electrolyte reabsorption occurs in this segment.

The maximum water absorption takes place in the jejunum.

The amount of water absorbed in the intestines follows this order: Jejunum > Ileum > Colon.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.

Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q031.displayText:
DMT1 transports ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) across the apical enterocyte membrane.

Transport of Fe2+ into the enterocytes occurs via divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1), through an active transport process.

Protein DMT-1 (Divalent Metal Transporter-1) is expressed on the apical surface of enterocytes in the initial part of the duodenum. DMT-1 is not specific to iron & transports other substances like zinc, copper, cobalt & manganese.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q001.displayText:
Principal cells and intercalated cells are characteristic of the late distal nephron: distal collecting tubule and collecting duct.

Principal cells and intercalated cells are present in the distal collecting tubule and the collecting duct.

Note: Principal cells are the primary site of action of potassium-sparing diuretics.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q002.displayText:
DCT tight junctions restrict paracellular movement, unlike the relatively leaky junctions of PCT; both segments retain basolateral Na⁺/K⁺ pumps.

DCT has 'tight' tight junctions, while PCT has 'leaky' tight junctions.

The 'tight' tight junctions can maintain the high electrochemical gradients produced by active transcellular transport. This property is used to produce either highly concentrated or diluted secretions, as in the distal nephron. Hence, it can produce urine with an osmolarity severalfold higher or lower than plasma.

In contrast, epithelia with 'leaky' tight junctions move large amounts of isosmotic fluid. A good example is transport in the proximal tubule.

Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase is present throughout most parts of the nephron.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q003.displayText:
Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops reaching deep into medulla and vasa recta, supporting concentrated urine.

In comparison to cortical nephrons, juxtamedullary nephrons are characterized by a long loop of Henle that descends deep into the inner medulla. It is essential for the concentration of urine.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q004.displayText:
At rest, the kidneys receive about one-fifth of cardiac output, roughly 1–1.2 L/min in an adult.

Kidneys receive approximately 20 to 28% of the cardiac output, which is approximately 1000 mL per minute.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q005.displayText:
Normal adult GFR is approximately 125 mL/min, or about 180 L/day.

The GFR in a healthy adult of average size is approximately 125 mL/min.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule per unit time.

The GFR is determined by:
• The sum of the hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces across the glomerular membrane, which gives the net filtration pressure
• The glomerular Kf (glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient)

Mathematically, it can be expressed as follows:
GFR = Kf × [forces favoring filtration − forces opposing filtration]
GFR = Kf × [PG + πB − PB − πG]

Forces favoring filtration:
• PG: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
• πB: Bowman's capsule oncotic pressure

Forces opposing filtration:
• PB: Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure
• πG: Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q006.displayText:
Resting renal blood flow is about 1–1.5 L/min, approximately 20–25% of cardiac output.

In a resting adult, the kidneys receive 1.2-1.3 L of blood per minute, or just under 25% of the cardiac output. Among the given options, 1-1.5 L/min is the closest range.

Renal blood flow is determined by the pressure gradient across the renal vasculature (the difference between the renal artery and renal vein hydrostatic pressures) divided by the total renal vascular resistance:
Renal blood flow = (Renal artery pressure − Renal vein pressure) / Total renal vascular resistance

Note: Renal blood flow = Renal plasma flow / (1 − Hematocrit).

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q008.displayText:
The filtration barrier is formed by fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms; mesangial cells are not a layer of it.

Mesangium does not form a filtration barrier. It is made up of mesangial cells, supporting the glomerular capillaries.

The filtration barrier consists of:
• Endothelium of the capillary
• Basement membrane:
• Lamina densa: an electron-dense layer. It contains type IV collagen.
• Lamina rara interna: contains the glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate, which has a negative charge.
• Lamina rara externa: contains the glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate, which has a negative charge.
• Layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q009.displayText:
For equal-sized particles, positive charge favors filtration because the glomerular barrier is negatively charged.

For any given molecular size, positively charged molecules are filtered much more readily than negatively charged molecules.

This is because the sialoproteins in the glomerular capillary wall are negatively charged, and this negative charge repels the negatively charged substances in the blood.

Studies have shown that, for tracer molecules presumed to be of similar size, the order of filtration by charge is positive charge > neutral charge > negative charge.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q010.displayText:
Neutral macromolecules with effective diameters around 4–8 nm are within the filtration barrier’s size-selective range.

Filtration barriers permit neutral substances that have a size of 4-8 nm.

Neutral substances with diameters:
• < 4 nm: freely filtered
• > 8 nm: not filtered
• Between 4-8 nm: the permeability is inversely proportional to the diameter

Clinical correlation:
• Genetically abnormal basement membranes: Alport's syndrome (α3 and α4 chains, on the long arm of chromosome 2, are involved in the autosomal dominant and recessive patterns; the α5 chain, on the X chromosome, is involved in X-linked inheritance)
• Autoimmune response to basement membrane collagen IV (α3 NC1 domain): Goodpasture's syndrome

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q011.displayText:
The juxtaglomerular apparatus includes macula densa, renin-secreting JG cells and extraglomerular mesangial (Lacis) cells.

Glomerular mesangial cells are not a part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

Juxtaglomerular apparatus contains:
• Macula densa: Specialized cells at the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle form the macula densa. They detect the sodium concentration of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, the macula densa cells trigger contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate.
• Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between the afferent and efferent arterioles.
• Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin. A fall in pressure in the afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

Note: The distal convoluted tubule starts at the macula densa.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q013.displayText:
Net filtration pressure = 45 − 20 − 10 + 0 = 15 mmHg; the oncotic pressure in Bowman space is normally negligible.

Net filtration pressure = Hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries − Pressure in Bowman's capsule − Oncotic pressure in the glomerular capillaries.

Net filtration pressure = PG − PB − πG + πB

Therefore, net filtration pressure = (45 − 10 − 20 + 0) = 15 mmHg.

Note: Here, just the net filtration pressure is asked and not the GFR: GFR = Kf × [PG − PB − πG + πB].

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q014.displayText:
Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals normal GFR: about 125 mL/min.

Inulin clearance is equal to 125 mL/min. Since it is used for the measurement of GFR, inulin clearance will be equal to GFR, i.e. 125 mL/min.

Renal clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per unit time.

A higher renal clearance suggests the substance may be cleared almost completely in one pass through the kidneys, while a low value describes a substance that may not be eliminated by the kidneys at all.

Clearance refers to the volume of plasma that would be necessary to supply the amount of substance excreted in the urine per unit of time. Stated mathematically:
Cx × Px = Ux × V
where Cx is the clearance rate of a substance x, Px is the plasma concentration of x, Ux is the urine concentration of x, and V is the urine flow rate.

Rearranging this equation, clearance can be expressed as:
Clearance = (Ux × V) / Px

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q015.displayText:
Inulin clearance equals GFR because the filtered inulin load is excreted unchanged without tubular handling.

In the given scenario, inulin clearance = GFR.

Inulin clearance is calculated by the formula:
C inulin = (U inulin × V) / P inulin

Substituting the values given:
• U inulin = 25 mg/mL
• V = 10 mL/min
• P inulin = 2 mg/mL

C inulin = (25 × 10) / 2 = 125 mL/min. Thus, inulin clearance = GFR (normal GFR = 125 mL/min).

Inulin is a polymer of fructose. Clearance of inulin can be used for measurement of GFR because of the following reasons:
• Freely filtered
• Neither reabsorbed nor secreted in the tubules
• Nontoxic
• Not metabolized by the body

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q016.displayText:
Clearance C = U×V/P = (100×2)/10 = 20 mL/min.

The clearance in the given scenario is 20 mL/min.

C = ([U]x × V) / [P]x
Where:
• C = clearance (mL/min)
• [U]x = urine concentration of substance x = 100 mg/mL
• V = urine flow rate = 2 mL/min
• [P]x = plasma concentration of substance x = 10 mg/mL

Substituting the values: C = (100 × 2) / 10 = 20 mL/min.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q017.displayText:
Renal sympathetic activation constricts afferent arterioles, lowering renal blood flow and GFR.

GFR decreases with sympathetic stimulation because of afferent arteriolar constriction.

Strong activation of the renal sympathetic nerves constricts the afferent and efferent arterioles through α1 receptors. As the afferent arterioles have far more α1 receptors than the efferent arterioles, the result is decreased renal blood flow and GFR.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q018.displayText:
A high-protein meal increases renal plasma flow and GFR through renal functional reserve and reduced afferent resistance.

High protein intake increases GFR.

Effect of protein intake on GFR: high dietary protein → ↑ amino acids → ↑ amino acid and NaCl reabsorption in the PCT (Na-amino acid cotransporter) → ↓ NaCl at the macula densa → macula densa feedback → ↓ afferent arteriolar resistance → ↑ GFR.

Note: An increase in the plasma protein concentration is not the same as high protein intake. An increase in the plasma protein concentration decreases GFR due to a raised oncotic pressure. A high protein intake raises the amino acid concentration in the blood, not the plasma protein concentration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q019.displayText:
Afferent arteriolar dilation raises both renal plasma flow and glomerular capillary pressure, increasing GFR.

Dilation of the afferent arteriole will increase both GFR and RPF:
• Renal plasma flow (RPF) increases, because renal vascular resistance is decreased.
• Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) increases, because glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is increased.
• Filtration fraction (FF) remains normal.

Dilation of the efferent arteriole will increase RPF but decrease GFR.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q020.displayText:
cAMP relaxes mesangial cells, increasing available filtration surface area; several vasoactive mediators contract them.

cAMP causes relaxation of the mesangial cells. The other agents mentioned in the options cause contraction of the mesangial cells.

Agents causing relaxation of mesangial cells (mnemonic: DAnCE):
• Dopamine
• ANP
• cAMP
• PGE2

Angiotensin II is an important regulator of mesangial contraction, and there are angiotensin II receptors in the glomeruli.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q021.displayText:
Renal prostaglandins preferentially preserve cortical perfusion while medullary flow falls, according to the source’s regional-flow description.

Prostaglandins increase blood flow in the renal cortex and decrease blood flow in the renal medulla.

PGE₂ is partly responsible for vasodilatation of the afferent arteriole, which increases blood flow to the glomerulus. This is why NSAIDs (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) result in afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. They can cause a reduced GFR in patients who rely heavily on prostaglandin synthesis to maintain renal blood flow.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q022.displayText:
The S3 segment of proximal tubule is especially vulnerable to ischemia because it lies in the outer medulla with high metabolic demand and relatively low oxygen supply.

The regions of the kidney most prone to ischemic injury are the S3 segment of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (mTAL). These tubular areas exist physiologically in relatively lower oxygen conditions.

The S3 segment, in particular, has a much lower capability of producing energy through glycolysis under anaerobic conditions than the mTAL.

Based on the ultrastructure, the proximal tubule is divided into three segments:
• S1 segment: 1st half of the PCT
• S2 segment: 2nd half of the PCT and 1st half of the proximal straight tubule
• S3 segment: 2nd half of the proximal straight tubule

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q023.displayText:
Effective renal plasma flow is approximately PAH clearance, about 625 mL/min in this calculation.

In humans, the effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) averages about 625 mL/min.

Measurement of renal plasma flow (RPF) is done by measuring the clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH). PAH is filtered and secreted by the renal tubules, hence it can be used for RPF measurement.

RPF = CPAH = (UPAH × V) / PPAH

where:
• RPF = renal plasma flow (mL/min or mL/24 hours)
• CPAH = clearance of PAH (mL/min or mL/24 hours)
• UPAH = urine concentration of PAH (mg/mL)
• V = urine flow rate (mL/min or mL/24 hours)
• PPAH = plasma concentration of PAH (mg/mL)

Note: Renal blood flow = Renal plasma flow / (1 − Hematocrit)

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q024.displayText:
Because ERPF = extraction ratio × true RPF, true RPF = ERPF / extraction ratio.

True renal plasma flow (RPF) is obtained by dividing effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) by the extraction ratio.

RPF = ERPF / Extraction ratio
where ERPF (effective renal plasma flow) = CPAH = (UPAH × V) / PPAH, and the extraction ratio is the percentage of PAH extracted by the kidney.

When we inject para-aminohippuric acid, 90% of it is cleared by the kidney at the rate of 625 mL per minute, which is the effective renal plasma flow (ERPF). To calculate the true RPF, we divide the ERPF by the extraction ratio (0.9) to account for the 10% that is not cleared, giving a final value of ~700 mL per minute.

When the peripheral venous plasma concentration of PAH is used for calculation of RPF, the RPF obtained is called the effective renal plasma flow (ERPF). This is because the PAH concentration is essentially identical to that in the arterial plasma reaching the kidney.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q026.displayText:
The myogenic response to stretch depolarizes afferent arteriolar smooth muscle and opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, causing contraction.

The afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch induced by the opening of calcium channels. The mechanism is called myogenic autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR.

The stretch of the vascular wall allows increased movement of calcium ions from the extracellular fluid into the cells, causing them to contract. This contraction prevents excessive stretch of the vessel. This prevents an excessive increase of renal blood flow and GFR by raising vascular resistance.

This mechanism may be more important in protecting the kidney from hypertension-induced injury.

Autoregulation has two main mechanisms:
• Metabolic mechanism: Tissues produce vasodilatory metabolites that regulate flow, e.g. prostaglandins, NO, CO₂, H⁺ and K⁺
• Myogenic mechanism

Myogenic autoregulation of renal blood flow: ↑ arterial wall tension (BP) → stretching of blood vessels (afferent arteriole smooth muscle) → opening of voltage-dependent calcium channels → calcium influx → increased intracellular calcium → vasoconstriction → prevents excessive increase of renal blood flow and GFR.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q027.displayText:
Macula densa NaCl delivery signals tubuloglomerular feedback and adjusts afferent tone and renin release.

Tubuloglomerular feedback is mediated by sensing of an increased Na⁺ concentration at the macula densa.

The macula densa is made of specialized cells at the distal end of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where it reaches the glomerulus. The distal convoluted tubule starts from the macula densa. The macula densa forms part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

While both Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are delivered to the macula densa cells, it is the increased concentration of Na⁺ in the cells that increases Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase activity, leading to the feedback.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q028.displayText:
Intrinsic renal autoregulation requires functional vascular smooth muscle; a denervated or isolated perfused kidney can still autoregulate.

Renal autoregulation is absent in case of paralysis of vascular smooth muscle.

Paralysis of vascular smooth muscle abolishes its action, i.e. autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR. Vascular smooth muscles act through the myogenic mechanism of renal autoregulation. Paralysis of vascular smooth muscles can be brought about by administration of drugs.

Renal autoregulation is present in denervated and in isolated, perfused kidneys.

Feedback mechanisms intrinsic to the kidneys keep the renal blood flow and GFR relatively constant, despite marked changes in arterial blood pressure. This relative constancy of GFR and renal blood flow is referred to as autoregulation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q030.displayText:
Tubuloglomerular feedback stabilizes single-nephron GFR by changing afferent tone and renin release in response to distal NaCl delivery.

Tubuloglomerular feedback regulates the glomerular filtration rate (GFR): as the rate of flow through the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the first part of the distal tubule increases, glomerular filtration in the same nephron decreases; conversely, a decrease in flow increases the GFR.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q031.displayText:
A freely filtered solute with zero efferent concentration has been removed from plasma by filtration across the glomerulus.

A concentration of 0 mg% in the efferent arteriole indicates the substance is freely filtered.

Afferent arterioles → glomerulus (filtration) → efferent arterioles → peritubular capillaries (reabsorption + secretion).

Note: The question compares the concentration in the afferent and efferent arterioles. Reabsorption and secretion happen between the tubular lumen of the nephron and the peritubular capillaries, and not the efferent arteriole.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q034.displayText:
A ureteric stone raises downstream tubular/Bowman pressure and opposes filtration, so it does not increase GFR.

A ureteric stone causes a reduction in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

Following ureteral obstruction, there is a progressive fall in GFR due to a reduction in the single-nephron glomerular filtration rate (SNGFR) and a reduced number of filtering nephrons.

All the other options increase GFR.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH34_Q035.displayText:
At equal size, dextran filterability ranks polycationic highest, neutral intermediate and polyanionic lowest because the GBM is negatively charged.

In the given graph, the order of filterability is A > B > C, which likely indicates that the substances are polycationic, neutral and polyanionic.

The glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged, which will repel most negatively charged (anionic) substances, whereas cationic substances are easily filtered. Hence, the order of filterability would be: polycationic > neutral > polyanionic, represented by A, B, and C in the graph shown.

The glomerular filtration barrier consists of:
• Endothelium of the capillary
• Basement membrane:
• Lamina densa: an electron-dense layer. It contains type IV collagen.
• Lamina rara interna: contains the glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate, which has a negative charge.
• Lamina rara externa: contains the glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate, which has a negative charge.
• Layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane

The capillary endothelium is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae, which measure from 4 nm up to 8 nm. Therefore, neutral substances with molecular diameters of less than 4 nm are freely filtered, and filtration of those with diameters of more than 8 nm approaches zero.

However, in addition to the size of the particles, filtration also depends mainly on the charge of the particle being filtered. The glomerular capillary wall consists of highly negatively charged proteins called sialoproteins, which repel the negatively charged substances (anions). This property can be studied by using charged dextran.

When the filtration of negatively and positively charged dextrans was studied, the results indicated that the negatively charged dextrans in the blood are repelled, with the result that filtration of anionic substances 4 nm in diameter is less than half that of neutral substances of the same size.

This explains why albumin, despite having an effective molecular diameter of approximately 7 nm, has a very low filtration rate.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q001.displayText:
Renal clearance above GFR indicates net tubular secretion, because filtered solute alone cannot clear plasma faster than filtration.

If a drug has a higher renal clearance than the GFR, the drug is secreted by the renal tubules.

Excretion rate = (filtration rate − reabsorption rate) + secretion rate.

The clearance of a substance:
• Equals the GFR if there is no net tubular secretion or reabsorption.
• Exceeds the GFR if there is net tubular secretion.
• Is less than the GFR if there is net tubular reabsorption.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q002.displayText:
Excretion rate is urine concentration (U) multiplied by urine flow (V); clearance divides this excretion rate by plasma concentration.

The correct formula is Excretion rate = UV.
• Filtration fraction = (GFR / RPF) × 100 = 20% (approximately 0.2)
• Filtration rate = GFR × plasma concentration
• Clearance = U × V / P

Where:
• GFR = glomerular filtration rate
• RPF = renal plasma flow
• U = concentration of the substance in urine
• V = urine flow rate
• P = concentration of the substance in plasma

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q003.displayText:
Creatinine is filtered and modestly secreted, so creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR.

Creatinine is partially secreted and never reabsorbed. Clearance of creatinine (CCr) can also be used to determine GFR. Since creatinine is secreted by the tubules, the clearance of creatinine will be slightly higher than that of inulin. Hence, it overestimates GFR.

Inulin is completely filtered and never reabsorbed. Hence, it can be used for GFR estimation.

Glucose is completely reabsorbed below the renal threshold (i.e. ~180 mg/dL) in the PCT.

PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) at low plasma concentrations is completely filtered and secreted. Hence, it can be used for estimation of renal blood flow.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q004.displayText:
Excess PAH saturates tubular secretion, lowering its extraction ratio and making PAH-based effective RPF falsely low.

Effective renal plasma flow in this patient will be falsely low.

It is equal to the clearance of para-aminohippurate (PAH), as shown by the following equation:
ERPF = (UPAH × V) / PPAH = CPAH

Where:
• ERPF = Effective renal plasma flow
• UPAH = [PAH] in urine
• V = Urine flow rate
• PPAH = [PAH] in plasma
• CPAH = Clearance of PAH

At high concentrations of PAH, as given in this question, tubular secretion attains saturation, after which the clearance of PAH falls. Hence, a low ERPF will be seen.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q005.displayText:
The thick ascending limb reabsorbs salt through the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2).

The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle has the Na⁺-2Cl⁻-K⁺ cotransporter, which cotransports one Na⁺, one K⁺, and 2 Cl⁻ from the tubular lumen into the tubular cells. This is an example of secondary active transport.

Na⁺ is transported out of the cell into the interstitium by Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase in the basolateral membrane of the cell.

Cl⁻ exits through basolateral ClC-Kb Cl⁻ channels. Barttin, a protein in the cell membrane, is essential for normal ClC-Kb function.

K⁺ moves from the cell to the interstitium and the tubular lumen through ROMK (renal outer medullary potassium channel) and other K⁺ channels.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q006.displayText:
The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered sodium, about two-thirds.

The principal site of absorption of Na⁺ is the PCT. About 60-65% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), coupled with the movement of H⁺, glucose, amino acids, organic acids, phosphate, and other electrolytes and substances.

All segments of the nephron are involved in sodium reabsorption except the thin descending limb of the loop of Henle.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q007.displayText:
Most filtered potassium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule; distal nephron potassium handling is variably regulated by secretion/reabsorption.

Potassium is maximally absorbed in the PCT.

Potassium is freely filtered by the glomerulus. The bulk of filtered K⁺ is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. In the proximal tubule, K⁺ absorption is primarily passive and proportional to Na⁺ and water, through paracellular transport.

K⁺ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of Henle occurs through both transcellular (Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransport) and paracellular pathways.

K⁺ secretion begins in the early distal convoluted tubule and progressively increases along the distal nephron into the cortical collecting duct. Most urinary K⁺ can be accounted for by K⁺ secretion mediated by principal cells. Under conditions of K⁺ depletion, reabsorption of K⁺ occurs in the collecting duct.

It is the only electrolyte to be reabsorbed as well as secreted.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q008.displayText:
Proximal bicarbonate reclamation begins with apical Na⁺–H⁺ exchange; secreted H⁺ titrates filtered bicarbonate in the lumen.

Bicarbonate is reabsorbed at the luminal membrane in the form of CO₂ and H₂O with the help of the Na⁺-H⁺ exchanger.

In the tubular cell of the PCT, CO₂ and H₂O recombine with the help of carbonic anhydrase II, and then dissociate into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. From here, the H⁺ moves back into the tubular lumen via the Na⁺-H⁺ exchanger, while the HCO₃⁻ is reabsorbed at the basolateral membrane via the Na⁺-HCO₃⁻ cotransporter.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q009.displayText:
Filtered amino acids are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by carrier-mediated transport.

Glucose and amino acids are completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

Option A: Maximum reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule.

Option B: Urea is reabsorbed and secreted. It is reabsorbed in the PCT and in the collecting duct. It is secreted in the thin ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

Option C: H⁺ is secreted in the PCT as well as in the collecting ducts.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q010.displayText:
Glucose enters proximal-tubule cells across the luminal membrane by sodium-glucose symport, using the Na⁺ gradient.

Sodium symport occurs along with glucose transport into the cell.

Sodium and glucose are cotransported across the luminal membrane of proximal tubular cells. This occurs via sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT2 and SGLT1). The energy derived from the movement of Na⁺ is used to move glucose against its concentration gradient into the tubular cell. This is referred to as secondary active transport.

The Na⁺ is then pumped out of the cell into the interstitium, and the glucose exits by facilitated diffusion via glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2) along the basolateral membrane into the interstitial fluid.

Clinical correlation:
• Fanconi-Bickel syndrome: Defective GLUT2
• Isolated renal glycosuria: Defective SGLT2

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q011.displayText:
The renal threshold for glucose is about 2 g/L and its transport maximum is about 375 mg/min.

The actual renal threshold is about 200 mg/dL (i.e. 2 g/L; 1 g/L = 100 mg/dL), and the transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min.

For substances that are actively reabsorbed or secreted, there is a limit to the rate at which the solute can be transported, which is referred to as the transport maximum. This limit is due to saturation of the specific transport systems involved.

Normally, measurable glucose does not appear in the urine because essentially all the filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

The transport maximum for glucose is about 375 mg/min, whereas the filtered load of glucose is only about 125 mg/min. With large increases in GFR and/or plasma glucose concentration that increase the filtered load of glucose above 375 mg/min, the excess glucose filtered is not reabsorbed and passes into the urine.

When the plasma glucose concentration is 100 mg/100 mL and the filtered load is at its normal level (125 mg/min), there is no loss of glucose in the urine. However, when the plasma concentration of glucose rises above about 200 mg/100 mL, increasing the filtered load to about 250 mg/min, a small amount of glucose begins to appear in the urine. This point is termed the threshold for glucose.

Splay is the separation between the filtered load and excretion curves. It occurs due to different transport maximums of different nephrons.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q012.displayText:
On the PAH excretion plot, filtered load appears first, secreted load adds to it, secretion reaches Tm, and excretion is the total urinary output.

The labels depicted are a. Filtered, b. Secreted, c. Tm, d. Excreted.

Filtered load: The filtered load of PAH increases linearly as the unbound concentration of PAH increases (filtered load = GFR × [P]PAH).

Secretion: At low concentrations of PAH, many carriers are available and secretion increases linearly as the plasma concentration increases. When the PAH concentration increases to a level where the carriers are saturated, Tm is reached. After this point, no matter how much the PAH concentration increases, there can be no further increase in the secretion rate.

Excretion: For a secreted substance such as PAH, excretion is the sum of filtration and secretion. At low PAH concentrations (below Tm), excretion increases steeply with increases in plasma PAH concentration, because both filtration and secretion are increasing. At PAH concentrations above Tm, excretion increases less steeply (and parallels the curve for filtration), because only the filtration component increases as concentration increases; secretion is already saturated.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q013.displayText:
With uncontrolled diabetes and plasma glucose above Tm, some glucose is excreted, so glucose clearance is greater than zero.

In uncontrolled diabetes, the plasma clearance of glucose is greater than zero.

Renal handling of glucose, inulin, and para-aminohippurate (PAH):
Glucose clearance: normally, all the glucose that is filtered is reabsorbed and no glucose is excreted in the urine, so the clearance is zero. In uncontrolled diabetes, the plasma glucose concentration exceeds the renal threshold for reabsorption, so excess glucose is excreted in the urine and the clearance is greater than zero.
Inulin clearance: inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Hence its clearance is constant and equal to the glomerular filtration rate.
PAH clearance: PAH is both filtered and secreted. When plasma PAH is low, clearance is high. As plasma PAH rises above the threshold level for PAH secretion, clearance falls progressively.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q014.displayText:
Filtered glucose = 2 mg/mL × 90 mL/min = 180 mg/min; excretion = filtered load − Tm, yielding 30 mg/min for the plotted Tm.

The amount of glucose excreted in the above scenario is 30 mg/min.

Calculation:

Step 1: Calculate the total filtered glucose. In this question:
• GFR = 90 mL/min
• Plasma glucose concentration = 200 mg/dL = 2 mg/mL (1 dL = 100 mL)
• Total filtered glucose = GFR × plasma glucose concentration = 90 mL/min × 2 mg/mL = 180 mg/min

Step 2: Check the transport maximum. In the above question, the transport maximum is 150 mg/min.

Step 3: Calculate the excretion. Excretion = Total filtered glucose − Total reabsorbed glucose (transport maximum) = 180 − 150 mg/min = 30 mg/min.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q015.displayText:
Urea concentration in proximal tubular fluid rises above plasma because water is reabsorbed more rapidly than urea.

The concentration of urea in tubular fluid is more than that of plasma.
• [TF/P] > 1 when the solute is reabsorbed less quickly than water or when the solute is secreted, e.g. PAH, creatinine, inulin, urea.
• [TF/P] = 1 when solute and water are reabsorbed at the same rate, e.g. Na⁺.
• [TF/P] < 1 when the solute is reabsorbed more quickly than water, e.g. glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q017.displayText:
ADH makes collecting ducts water-permeable, allowing water reabsorption into hyperosmotic medulla and concentrated urine.

Hypertonic urine is excreted due to absorption of water in the collecting duct.

The final concentration of urine is determined by the amount of water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts. Whether the urine is hypotonic or hypertonic depends on the amount of ADH (vasopressin) acting on the collecting ducts.

The basic requirements for forming a concentrated (hypertonic) urine are:
• A high level of ADH, which increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water, allowing these segments to avidly reabsorb water.
• A high osmolarity of the renal medullary interstitial fluid, which provides the osmotic gradient necessary for water reabsorption in the presence of high levels of ADH.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q018.displayText:
Vasopressin acts maximally on collecting-duct V₂ receptors to insert aquaporin-2 and increase water reabsorption.

Vasopressin has the maximum effect on the collecting ducts.

Vasopressin acts by inserting aquaporin 2, present in cytoplasmic vesicles of principal cells, into the apical membrane. The effect is mediated via the vasopressin V2 receptor, cyclic adenosine 3',5'-monophosphate (cAMP), and protein kinase A. When vasopressin is absent, the collecting duct epithelium is relatively impermeable to water.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q021.displayText:
The thick ascending limb is essentially impermeable to water; its salt reabsorption dilutes tubular fluid.

The thick ascending limb is always impermeable to H₂O.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q022.displayText:
Urine osmolality ranges broadly from about 100 to 800 mOsm/kg depending on hydration and ADH.

The average urine osmolality is 100-800 mosm/kg.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q025.displayText:
Medullary hyperosmolarity is largely generated by NaCl, especially from loop salt transport; urea also contributes in the inner medulla.

Hyperosmolarity of the medullary interstitium is mainly due to NaCl and urea.

The major factors that contribute to the build-up of solute concentration in the renal medulla are:
• Active transport of Na⁺ and co-transport of K⁺, Cl⁻, and other ions out of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle into the medullary interstitium.
• Active transport of ions from the collecting ducts into the medullary interstitium.
• Facilitated diffusion of urea from the inner medullary collecting ducts into the medullary interstitium; this urea reabsorption is increased in the presence of ADH.
• Diffusion of only small amounts of water from the medullary tubules into the medullary interstitium.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q026.displayText:
Countercurrent multiplication occurs in the loop of Henle and is preserved by vasa recta exchange; the PCT is not part of the countercurrent mechanism.

The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) does not play a role in the countercurrent mechanism.

The countercurrent mechanism consists of 2 components:
• Countercurrent multiplier: (a) absorption of water via aquaporin-1 in the thin descending limb; (b) active Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ transport in the thick ascending limb; (c) flow of fluid from the PCT to the DCT.
• Countercurrent exchanger: the vasa recta are involved in this process. They help maintain the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla. This is a passive process.

Urea build-up in the renal medulla also contributes to the medullary osmotic gradient.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q027.displayText:
Maximum papillary osmolality depends on loop length, ascending salt transport and descending-limb water permeability.

The maximum osmolality that can be reached at the tip of the medulla is proportional to the length of the loop of Henle, because the loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier to maintain the gradient in the medulla. The greater the length of the loop of Henle, the greater the osmolality that can be reached at the tip of the medulla.

In the case of juxtamedullary nephrons with longer loops and thin ascending limbs, the osmotic gradient is spread over a greater distance and the osmolality at the tip of the loop is greater.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q028.displayText:
Countercurrent blood exchange occurs in kidney vasa recta and testicular pampiniform plexus, not the eye.

The eye does not have a countercurrent blood flow system.

Heat and substances, including gases, steroids and peptide hormones, can pass from venous blood, interstitial fluid and lymph to the arterial blood; the process is called local countercurrent transfer.

Examples of countercurrent blood flow:
• Heat exchange between the arteries and venae comitantes of the limbs
• Vasa recta in the kidneys
• Testes
• Small intestine

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q029.displayText:
The thin ascending limb is relatively impermeable to water and passive NaCl reabsorption is not the classic driving component; its asserted sodium outflow is the exception.

Thin ascending limb is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism.

The loops of Henle function as countercurrent multipliers and the vasa recta as countercurrent exchangers.

The functioning of the loop of Henle depends upon:
• High permeability of the thin descending limb to water (via aquaporin-1)
• Active transport of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the thick ascending limb
• Inflow of tubular fluid from the proximal tubule and outflow to the distal tubule

Note: The thin ascending limbs of juxtamedullary nephrons are permeable to Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and hence do contribute passively to countercurrent multiplication. However, among the options provided, Option C is the best answer, as the other options are directly responsible for the countercurrent mechanism.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q030.displayText:
The thick ascending limb is the diluting segment because it reabsorbs NaCl while remaining impermeable to water.

The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is called the diluting segment.

In the ascending limb, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ move out of the tubular lumen, and the tubular fluid becomes more dilute. When the fluid reaches the top of the ascending limb, it is hypotonic to plasma.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q031.displayText:
Chloride concentration rises along the PCT as water and bicarbonate are reabsorbed; amino acids, glucose and bicarbonate concentrations decline.

As the filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the concentration of chloride increases.
• The concentration of chloride in the early part of the PCT is ~105 mEq/L.
• As sodium is reabsorbed, it preferentially carries glucose, amino acids, and bicarbonate with it.
• This leaves behind a solution that has a higher concentration of chloride, which, as it reaches the second half of the PCT, is ~140 mEq/L.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH35_Q032.displayText:
Macula densa cells are specialized epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule that sense tubular NaCl.

Macula densa is formed by specialized tubular epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus consists of the following parts:
• Macula densa: At the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle, and at the beginning of the distal tubule, the tubular epithelial cells are specialized to form the macula densa. They detect the sodium concentration of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, the macula densa cells trigger contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate. This happens as follows: when there is increased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity, which leads to increased ATP hydrolysis, causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densa cells stimulate them to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, thereby decreasing the GFR.
• Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between the afferent and efferent arterioles.
• Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin. A fall in pressure in the afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH36_Q016.displayText:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II predominantly on pulmonary endothelial surfaces.

Sites of activation:
• Angiotensin I → angiotensin II: lungs
• Cholecalciferol → 25-hydroxyvitamin D3: liver
• 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 → 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3: kidney

Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), which is expressed in the lungs.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q004.displayText:
Only cones occupy the foveola; peripheral retina is rod-rich and more sensitive but less acute.

Source explanation detail: Central fovea (foveola) contains only cones (rod-free area) and is a region of highest resolution.

Regional variations in the retina:

Macula lutea:
• Located at the posterior pole, temporal to the optic disc
• Area of central vision
• High density of photoreceptors and interneurons

Optic disc:
• Lacks photoreceptors
• Is called the "blind spot"
• Normally a person is unaware of the blind spot because the corresponding part of the visual field can be seen by the contralateral eye, and neurological processes complete the incomplete image perceptually

Peripheral retina:
• Higher ratio of rods to cones (rod to cone ratio 20:1)
• Greater degree of convergence of photoreceptors onto the target interneuron (bipolar cells)
• More sensitivity to light
• Lower visual acuity

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q005.displayText:
Light closes outer-segment cGMP-gated channels, so the rod hyperpolarizes.

Source explanation detail: The rod receptor potential differs from other surface receptors in that it shows hyperpolarization.

In most sensory receptors: arrival of stimulus → ion channels are opened, allowing current to flow → depolarisation of the receptor.

In photoreceptors: when light strikes the outer segment, a cascade of reactions is initiated that closes some of the Na⁺ channels in the outer segment and results in hyperpolarization.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q012.displayText:
LGN input to primary visual cortex chiefly terminates in layer 4.

Source explanation detail: The axons from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) mostly end in layer 4.

The primary visual receiving area (primary visual cortex) is located principally on the sides of the calcarine fissure and has 6 layers, similar to the neocortex. Layer 4 receives most of the input from the LGN, and is divided further into 4A, 4B, 4Cα and 4Cβ.

The magnocellular pathway from layers 1 and 2 of the LGN ends in layer 4Cα, while the parvocellular pathway from layers 3-6 of the LGN ends in layer 4Cβ.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q013.displayText:
Protanopia is the red-deficiency form of dichromatic color vision.

Source explanation detail: Protanopes are dichromats with difficulty in identifying the colour red.

Anomalous trichromatic vision:
• Deficiency of red is protanomaly.
• Deficiency of green is deuteranomaly.
• Deficiency of blue is tritanomaly.

Dichromatic vision (individuals with only two cone systems):
• Blindness to red is protanopia (protanope).
