• Blindness to green is deuteranopia (deuteranope).
• Blindness to blue is tritanopia (tritanope).

Monochromatic vision: only one cone system.

Colour blindness is X-linked recessive. Achromatopsia (achromasia) is colour blindness due to lesions of area V8 of the visual cortex.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q015.displayText:
Binaural direction detection begins in the superior olivary complex.

Source explanation detail: The superior olivary nuclei receive information from both ears and begin the process of detecting the direction from which a sound comes.

The eighth nerves reach their respective cochlear nuclei in the medulla, from where fibres travel to both the ipsilateral and contralateral superior olivary nuclei in the pons, giving the ability to detect the direction of the sound.

The lateral part of the superior olivary nucleus does so by comparing the difference in intensities of sound reaching the two ears, whereas the medial part of the superior olivary nucleus detects the time lag between the signals entering the two ears.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q016.displayText:
Greater basilar-membrane vibration amplitude signals a louder sound.

Source explanation detail: There are at least three ways in which the auditory system determines loudness:
• As the sound becomes louder, the amplitude of vibration of the basilar membrane increases, so that the hair cells excite the nerve endings at more rapid rates.
• As the amplitude increases, more and more hair cells on the fringes of the resonating portion of the basilar membrane become stimulated.
• As the amplitude of vibration reaches high intensity, the outer hair cells become recruited at a significant rate.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q018.displayText:
Mitral cells are projection neurons in the olfactory bulb.

Source explanation detail: Mitral cells are seen in the olfactory bulb.

Axons of the olfactory nerves (first cranial nerve) synapse with the mitral cells and tufted cells in the olfactory bulb to form anatomically discrete units called olfactory glomeruli.

The olfactory bulb also contains periglomerular cells, which are inhibitory interneurons, and granule cells, which make reciprocal synapses with mitral and tufted cells.

These mitral and tufted cells (second-order neurons) terminate in the olfactory cortex.

In Southern blotting, DNA fragments are first separated by electrophoresis.
• The DNA in the gel is then made single-stranded by exposure to dilute alkali, and transferred by capillary action to the nylon membrane, which is laid over it. The relative positions of the different DNA fragments are thus preserved on the membrane.
• The membrane is then soaked in buffer containing the labelled probe, which base pairs with the DNA fragment of interest.
• The position of that fragment is then determined by autoradiography (exposure of the membrane to X-ray film) or fluorescent detection of the hybridized probe.

Southern blotting: electrophoresis is used to separate DNA fragments by size; there can be so many fragments that they appear as a smear on the gel. The DNA is transferred from the agarose gel to a nylon membrane. The membrane is bathed in a solution containing a probe, a short piece of DNA complementary to the sequence of interest. The probe is labeled or tagged with a fluorescent dye so that the location of DNA fragments to which it hybridizes can be visualized.

In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal. Hence, both 1 and 2 are correct.

• In obstructive lung diseases, both FEV1 and FVC are reduced, and the decrease in FEV1 is more than the reduction in FVC. As a result, the FEV1/FVC ratio also decreases.
• The total lung capacity is usually normal in chronic bronchitis, while it is increased in emphysema.
• Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the volume of air present in the lungs at the end of passive expiration. In COPD, FRC is increased.

Lung Capacities:
The total lung capacity can be broken down into capacities that help to define lung function.
• The vital capacity is the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung, or maximum inspiratory level.
• The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level.
• The functional residual capacity is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath. FRC = expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.
